The manager-generated worker Pod does not currently propagate imagePullSecrets. The September Alpha scaffold must therefore use an image that cluster nodes can pull without a private-registry Secret. Defining a least-privilege propagation and rotation contract is required before private worker registries are supported.

Projected credential, CA, and intent-Secret volumes update in place. The optional CA is mounted as the live directory /var/run/secrets/cisco-vk/controller-ca, not as a subPath file, so kubelet can publish a ConfigMap rotation without restarting the worker. The worker's generic projected-material watcher polls Kubernetes AtomicWriter ..data symlinks every five seconds without reading or hashing values. It passes adapters a coalescing Options.MaterialRotation.Changes channel and a fifteen-minute MaxSessionLifetime.

An adapter must consume that single channel once and fan it out internally if it has multiple reconcilers. On notification it must discard cached authentication, TLS, and resolved-intent state, re-read the mounted files, and requeue affected work before its next external request. Independently, it must rebuild clients and sessions by the maximum lifetime even if no event arrives. Caching credential or CA bytes only at process start is non-conforming.

docs.title: Intent Secret authorization
docs.text:
Secret selection is deliberately split across two authorization domains:

  1. An administrator who can modify NetworkController defines spec.intentSecretSources, mapping an alias to one same-namespace Secret name/key.
  2. A configuration author uses NetworkControllerConfig.spec.secretRefs[].source to select only that alias and its destination section/path. The config object cannot name a Secret or key.
  3. The manager translates only approved aliases into read-only projected files. This path writes references into the Pod specification and does not inspect Secret .data; the kubelet resolves the projection. The shared manager's separate cluster-wide Secret watch can still place typed Secret objects in its cache, so its RBAC and memory remain part of the credential trust boundary described in Security.

This prevents a configuration reconciler from turning the manager into a Secret-read deputy. The boundary is effective only when Kubernetes RBAC reserves NetworkController creation and updates for administrators while delegating NetworkControllerConfig separately to configuration authors.

An unknown alias, invalid section/path, or excess projection invalidates only that projection. The manager skips it and emits a sanitized IntentSecretProjectionSkipped warning/event; it does not write NetworkControllerConfig status. A missing or otherwise unresolved projected file is optional at Pod-mount time, so the adapter skips the affected config and reports IntentSecretsReady=False through that config's status. Neither case quiesces the endpoint worker or blocks other valid configs. Status and drift reports identify aliases, redacted paths, and change types only—never Secret names, keys, or values.

Server certificate verification is enabled by default. A custom CA is supplied through tls.caConfigMapRef; insecureSkipVerify is a lab/migration escape hatch and must not be the production default. Future adapter-specific RBAC must be a separately reviewed static ClusterRole selected by its descriptor, accepted by the registry's closed role allow-list, and added to the manager's matching bind policy—not dynamically generated rules or a broadening of the base role. Additional roles must not grant workers update/patch on the main NetworkController or NetworkControllerConfig resources or access to their finalizers.

docs.title: Adding a controller adapter
docs.text:
Adding a product integration should normally require no generic CRD change:

  1. Choose the upstream controller-centric Network as Code stripe. Record the exact format, qualified model versions, supported top-level sections, and source fixtures.
  2. Implement a package below the controller adapter tree. Keep its native API types and client private to that package.
  3. Implement the generic adapter lifecycle. Construction validates local options only; it must not dial the endpoint or start goroutines. Register reconcilers and manager-owned runnables during adapter setup so cancellation and shutdown follow the worker context.
  4. Register one immutable descriptor and factory. Descriptors use a stable, DNS-label controller type, a netascode-* model format, bounded unique capabilities/sections, and an audited worker ClusterRole name.
  5. Import the adapter only from cmd/cisco-vk/controller_adapters_register.go. The manager may read the registered descriptor, but it must never invoke the factory. Do not add product branches to the neutral registry, manager reconciler, per-device driver factory, or existing transport packages.
  6. Add conformance tests for common contract-gate ordering, IntentSecretsReady failure handling, descriptor validation, model/version rejection, report-before-apply behavior, section ownership, idempotency, async task recovery, redaction, credential rotation, TLS verification, rate limiting, and cancellation.
  7. If the adapter needs Kubernetes permissions beyond the base worker role, add a static least-privilege ClusterRole and an explicit manager-side allowlist entry. Explain and test every extra resource and verb. Never add Secret reads or mutation of controller/config specs, metadata, or finalizers.

Registration is a build-time contract, not runtime configuration. Invalid or duplicate descriptors stop process initialization; an unregistered NetworkController.spec.type produces no worker. The manager passes the selected descriptor digest into the Pod, and the worker refuses to start if its compiled registration differs. This makes accidentally mixing manager and adapter images fail closed instead of silently changing model, capability, or RBAC behavior.

The acceptance bar is that removing the adapter package and its composition- root import leaves the generic APIs, registry, manager, worker, existing device drivers, and transports building and behaving identically.

docs.title: Reference adapters
docs.text:
• Catalyst SD-WAN: sdwan, fixture-qualified NetworkControllerConfig apply against SD-WAN Manager.
  • Nexus Dashboard: nexus-dashboard, health, inventory and opt-in CiscoDevice adoption; no ND configuration management.

docs.title: CRD Reference
docs.text: Cisco Virtual Kubelet is operated primarily through Kubernetes custom resources. This page maps the CRDs shipped by the chart to their purpose, controller boundary, and common operator workflow.

docs.title: CRDs At A Glance
docs.text:
$ kubectl api-resources | grep -E 'cisco|iosxe|nxos|deviceoperations'
NAME                         SHORTNAMES      APIVERSION                  NAMESPACED   KIND
ciscodevices                 cvk             cisco.vk/v1alpha1          true         CiscoDevice
networkcontrollers           netctrl         cisco.vk/v1alpha1          true         NetworkController
networkcontrollerconfigs     nccfg           config.cisco.vk/v1alpha1   true         NetworkControllerConfig
iosxeconfigs                 iosxecfg        config.cisco.vk/v1alpha1   true         IOSXEConfig
nxosconfigs                  nxoscfg         config.cisco.vk/v1alpha1   true         NXOSConfig
iosxeconfigdefaults          iosxedefaults   config.cisco.vk/v1alpha1   false        IOSXEConfigDefaults
iosxedevicegroupconfigs      iosxegroup      config.cisco.vk/v1alpha1   true         IOSXEDeviceGroupConfig
iosxeinterfacegroupconfigs   iosxeifgroup    config.cisco.vk/v1alpha1   true         IOSXEInterfaceGroupConfig
iosxetemplates               iosxetpl        config.cisco.vk/v1alpha1   true         IOSXETemplate
iosxeconfigbundles           iosxebundle     config.cisco.vk/v1alpha1   true         IOSXEConfigBundle
iosxeconfigrevisions         iosxerev        config.cisco.vk/v1alpha1   true         IOSXEConfigRevision
iosxeconfigapplylogs         iosxelog        config.cisco.vk/v1alpha1   true         IOSXEConfigApplyLog
iosxediagnostics             iosxediag       config.cisco.vk/v1alpha1   true         IOSXEDiagnostic
iosxetelemetries             iosxetel        config.cisco.vk/v1alpha1   true         IOSXETelemetry
deviceoperations             devop           ops.cisco.vk/v1alpha1      true         DeviceOperation
iosxeoperationalactions      xeop            ops.cisco.vk/v1alpha1      true         IOSXEOperationalAction
iosxesoftwareupgrades        xeupgrade       ops.cisco.vk/v1alpha1      true         IOSXESoftwareUpgrade
iosxesoftwarerollouts        xerollout       ops.cisco.vk/v1alpha1      true         IOSXESoftwareRollout

CRD maturity

All CRDs are currently versioned v1alpha1. CRDs marked Beta below cover feature areas that are functional and tested but whose schemas and behaviours are still stabilising. Evaluate them in non-production environments before broader rollout. CRDs marked Stable cover the core pod-hosting and device-management surface that has been in service across multiple releases. CRDs marked Alpha define a tested generic extension boundary with two adapters of limited, documented scope: Catalyst SD-WAN Manager (fixture-qualified) and Nexus Dashboard. Experimental marks opt-in, controlled-evaluation workflows whose qualification limits must be reviewed before use.

Kind Scope Maturity Primary use CiscoDevice Namespaced Stable Declares one managed device and drives the per-device VK deployment. NetworkController Namespaced Alpha Declares one external controller endpoint and its isolated worker contract. Adapter types: sdwan and nexus-dashboard; a type with no adapter creates no worker. nexus-dashboard can also adopt its switches as CiscoDevice objects through the opt-in spec.deviceAdoption. NetworkControllerConfig Namespaced Alpha Carries resolved, versioned controller-centric Network as Code intent. Consumed by the sdwan adapter, which can apply to SD-WAN Manager when spec.mode: apply is selected; Retain is the only deletion policy, so remote pruning and deletion are not implemented. The nexus-dashboard adapter does not consume it. IOSXEConfigDefaults Cluster Beta Fleet-wide baseline configuration merged into device intent. IOSXEDeviceGroupConfig Namespaced Beta Shared configuration for selected devices. IOSXEInterfaceGroupConfig Namespaced Beta Shared configuration for selected interfaces on selected devices. IOSXETemplate Namespaced Beta Reusable parameterized configuration fragments. IOSXEConfig Namespaced Beta Per-device Network as Code intent, drift detection, apply, and rollback. NXOSConfig Namespaced Beta Per-device NX-OS Network as Code intent over NX-API REST/DME for system, feature, feature_set, vlan, and interface_ethernet. IOSXEConfigBundle Namespaced Beta Fans one config template out across selected devices. IOSXEConfigRevision Namespaced Beta Immutable resolved-intent history used for rollback and audit. IOSXEConfigApplyLog Namespaced Beta Per-apply audit entries with family and diff metadata. IOSXEDiagnostic Namespaced Beta Read-only command capture, one-shot or scheduled. IOSXETelemetry Namespaced Beta gNMI subscriptions mapped to OpenTelemetry signals. DeviceOperation Namespaced Beta Auditable read-only operational requests, including gNOI probes. IOSXEOperationalAction Namespaced Beta One-shot write-class gNOI actions with confirmation and events. Requires --enable-write-class-gnoi. IOSXESoftwareUpgrade Namespaced Beta Multi-phase gNOI software install, activate, verify, and rollback. Requires --enable-iosxesoftwareupgrade. IOSXESoftwareRollout Namespaced Experimental Manager-owned, topology-aware software campaigns that create per-device IOSXESoftwareUpgrade objects. Disabled by default; requires managed topology and the software-upgrade gate.

docs.title: CiscoDevice
docs.text:
CiscoDevice is the inventory and lifecycle root. The manager watches it, creates or updates a per-device VK deployment, and that VK registers a virtual node that can host Kubernetes pods through device App-Hosting.

Use it when you want Kubernetes to see a Cisco device as a schedulable node. Important fields include spec.driver, spec.address, spec.credentialSecretRef, spec.transport, spec.gnoi, spec.xe.gnoi, spec.configPrereqs, and spec.opsPolicy.

apiVersion: cisco.vk/v1alpha1
kind: CiscoDevice
metadata:
  name: cat9300-4
  labels:
    site: lab
    role: access
spec:
  driver: XE
  address: 198.51.100.104
  port: 443
  username: cisco
  credentialSecretRef:
    name: cat9300-4-credentials
  transport: restconf
  maxPods: 16
  xe:
    networking:
      interface:
        type: AppGigabitEthernet
        appGigabitEthernet:
          mode: trunk
          vlanIf:
            dhcp: true
            vlan: 300
            guestInterface: 0

For secure gNOI transport and opt-in certificate provisioning, see the configuration reference and the secure gNOI workflow. Kubernetes-specific gNOI trust uses a same-namespace spec.gnoi.tls.secretRef; local certificate paths are rejected by admission. Choose either that generic trust source or spec.xe.gnoi.certificateProvisioning, not both.

$ kubectl get cvk
NAME        DRIVER   ADDRESS          PHASE   AGE
cat9300-4   XE       198.51.100.104   Ready   42m

$ kubectl get nodes -l cisco.io/device=cat9300-4
NAME        STATUS   ROLES   AGE   VERSION
cat9300-4   Ready    agent   41m   v1.30.0-vk

docs.title: Network controller scaffold (Alpha)
docs.text:
NetworkController (cisco.vk/v1alpha1) defines an HTTPS controller endpoint, credential and trust references, neutral connection limits, and an open adapter type. NetworkControllerConfig (config.cisco.vk/v1alpha1) targets that endpoint with resolved, explicitly versioned controller-centric Network as Code intent and section ownership. The controller type and endpoint form an immutable stable identity; credentials and TLS trust may rotate in place. Moving to a replacement endpoint requires a new NetworkController and explicit config retargeting so asynchronous task and ownership state cannot be replayed against another controller.

These CRDs are a generic extension API, not a claim of built-in support for Catalyst Center or any other controller. Two adapters are registered:

  • sdwan (Catalyst SD-WAN) is a fixture-qualified increment, not full NetAsCode parity. It applies intent to SD-WAN Manager only when spec.mode: apply is selected; remote pruning and deletion are not implemented (Retain).
  • nexus-dashboard (Nexus Dashboard) reports health, ND version and switch inventory. With the opt-in spec.deviceAdoption, it creates standalone CiscoDevice objects for reachable NX-OS switches; it never changes ND configuration and has no NetworkControllerConfig support yet.

A spec.type with no registered adapter fails closed and creates no worker. Duplicate fencing compares the exact stored endpoint string only within one namespace, which remains the Kubernetes trust and RBAC boundary. See the Network Controller Extension Guide for the registration, isolation, lifecycle, and security contracts.

docs.title: Configuration CRDs
docs.text:
Beta

The device configuration CRDs below are Beta (v1alpha1). Their schemas, managed families, and drift-detection behaviour are still expanding. Evaluate in non-production environments before broader rollout.

The IOS-XE configuration CRDs work together. Defaults, groups, interface groups, templates, and per-device source are resolved into canonical intent. The config driver plans the change, applies managed families, verifies drift, and records history. NXOSConfig uses the same common reconciliation contract for per-device NX-OS intent, but starts with a narrower family set over NX-API REST/DME.

Typical flow:

IOSXEConfigDefaults
  + IOSXEDeviceGroupConfig
  + IOSXEInterfaceGroupConfig
  + IOSXETemplate
  + IOSXEConfig / IOSXEConfigBundle
  -> resolved intent
  -> managed family writers
  -> RESTCONF, NETCONF, or gNMI transport
  -> IOS-XE running config
  -> status, revision, and apply log

NXOSConfig
  -> managed family writers
  -> NX-API transport
  -> NX-OS running config
  -> status and verify result

docs.title: IOSXEConfigDefaults
docs.text:
IOSXEConfigDefaults is cluster-scoped baseline intent. Use it for fleet-wide configuration that should apply before namespace or device-specific overrides.

apiVersion: config.cisco.vk/v1alpha1
kind: IOSXEConfigDefaults
metadata:
  name: enterprise-baseline
spec:
  configuration:
    ntp:
      servers:
        - address: 192.0.2.10
    aaa:
      new_model: true

docs.title: IOSXEDeviceGroupConfig
docs.text:
IOSXEDeviceGroupConfig selects devices by explicit references or labels and contributes shared intent. Use it for site, role, or platform configuration.

apiVersion: config.cisco.vk/v1alpha1
kind: IOSXEDeviceGroupConfig
metadata:
  name: lab-access
spec:
  deviceSelector:
    matchLabels:
      site: lab
      role: access
  configuration:
    logging:
      hosts:
        - 192.0.2.30

docs.title: IOSXEInterfaceGroupConfig
docs.text:
IOSXEInterfaceGroupConfig applies shared intent to matching interfaces on matching devices. Use it for repeated switchport, VLAN, trunk, or management patterns.

apiVersion: config.cisco.vk/v1alpha1
kind: IOSXEInterfaceGroupConfig
metadata:
  name: app-hosting-uplinks
spec:
  deviceSelector:
    matchLabels:
      role: access
  interfaceSelector:
    - type: GigabitEthernet
      namePattern: "1/0/[1-4]"
  configuration:
    interface_ethernet:
      interfaces:
        - description: "Kubernetes app-hosting access"
          enabled: true

docs.title: IOSXETemplate
docs.text:
IOSXETemplate stores reusable fragments. Templates keep common intent in one place and let IOSXEConfig inject values from the target device or namespace.

apiVersion: config.cisco.vk/v1alpha1
kind: IOSXETemplate
metadata:
  name: snmp-site-template
spec:
  parameters:
    - name: site
      type: string
      required: true
  configuration:
    snmp_server:
      location: "{{ .site }}"

docs.title: IOSXEConfig
docs.text:
IOSXEConfig is the main per-device declarative configuration CRD. Use it for managed YANG families, drift detection, dry-run style planning, transaction mode, source version selection, and rollback.

apiVersion: config.cisco.vk/v1alpha1
kind: IOSXEConfig
metadata:
  name: cat9300-4-network
spec:
  deviceRef:
    name: cat9300-4
  managedFamilies:
    - dhcp
    - vlan
  driftPolicy: report
  writeStartup: true
  source:
    inline:
      vlan:
        vlans:
          - id: 300
            name: APP_HOSTING
      dhcp:
        pools:
          - name: app-hosting
            network: 10.30.0.0
            mask: 255.255.255.0
            default_router: 10.30.0.1

$ kubectl get iosxecfg
NAME                 DEVICE      PHASE    DRIFT   AGE
cat9300-4-network    cat9300-4   InSync   none    17m

Full status when in sync:

$ kubectl describe iosxeconfig cat9300-4-network
...
Status:
  Conditions:
    Last Transition Time:  2026-05-30T10:00:42Z
    Message:               all managed families in sync
    Reason:                InSync
    Status:                True
    Type:                  Ready
  Family Statuses:
    - Family:   dhcp
      Phase:    InSync
    - Family:   vlan
      Phase:    InSync
  Phase:        InSync
  Revision Ref:
    Name:  cat9300-4-network-v4
Events:
  Type    Reason   Age   Message
  ----    ------   ----  -------
  Normal  Applied  17m   families [dhcp vlan] applied in 1.2s, 0 drift

When drift is detected with driftPolicy: report:

$ kubectl get iosxecfg
NAME                 DEVICE      PHASE    DRIFT     AGE
cat9300-4-network    cat9300-4   Drifted  [vlan]    23m

$ kubectl describe iosxeconfig cat9300-4-network
...
Status:
  Family Statuses:
    - Family:  dhcp
      Phase:   InSync
    - Family:  vlan
      Phase:   Drifted
      Drift Summary: |
        observed vlan 300 name: "changed-externally"
        desired  vlan 300 name: "APP_HOSTING"
  Phase:  Drifted
Events:
  Type     Reason   Age  Message
  ----     ------   ---  -------
  Warning  Drifted  2m   family vlan: 1 leaf divergence detected (driftPolicy=report, no patch sent)

IOSXEConfigApplyLog records each apply attempt for audit:

$ kubectl get iosxelog -l config.cisco.vk/config=cat9300-4-network
NAME                         DEVICE      FAMILIES   RESULT    AGE
cat9300-4-network-20260530   cat9300-4   dhcp,vlan   Applied   17m

$ kubectl describe iosxeconfigapplylog cat9300-4-network-20260530
...
Spec:
  Config Ref:  cat9300-4-network
  Device Ref:  cat9300-4
  Families:    [dhcp, vlan]
Status:
  Applied At:  2026-05-30T10:00:42Z
  Duration:    1.2s
  Op Count:    3
  Result:      Applied
  Revision Ref:
    Name:  cat9300-4-network-v4

docs.title: NXOSConfig
docs.text:
NXOSConfig is the per-device declarative configuration CRD for NX-OS. It uses the common config runtime, fetches observed state through NX-API, applies managed families, and verifies the post-apply state before reporting InSync. The first supported families are system, feature, feature_set, vlan, and interface_ethernet. The strict imported source is a flattened per-device canonical family map. A full nxos: envelope is accepted only for native CVK-authored compatibility sources that omit modelSource; it must not be labelled resolved: true. Unsupported fields inside implemented families fail closed at writer diff time.

apiVersion: config.cisco.vk/v1alpha1
kind: NXOSConfig
metadata:
  name: nexus9300v-network
spec:
  deviceRef:
    name: nexus9300v-01
  managedFamilies:
    - system
    - vlan
    - interface_ethernet
  driftPolicy: report
  modelSource:
    format: netascode-nxos
    modelVersion: 0.3.0
    schemaDigest: sha256:5d5482679fb28e751d34cdc49342f8434914a7714966ba8244923b95d678698d
    resolved: true
    exporter: example-customer-exporter@0123456789abcdef0123456789abcdef01234567
    sourceRevision: 0123456789abcdef0123456789abcdef01234567
  source:
    inline:
      system:
        hostname: nexus9300v-01
      vlan:
        vlans:
          - id: 3903
            name: CVK_LAB
      interfaces:
        ethernets:
          - id: 1/1
            description: CVK uplink
            shutdown: false
            mtu: 9216

$ kubectl get nxoscfg
NAME                  DEVICE          PHASE    DRIFT    AGE
nexus9300v-network    nexus9300v-01   InSync   report   2m

docs.title: IOSXEConfigBundle, Revision, and ApplyLog
docs.text:
IOSXEConfigBundle fans one IOSXEConfig template out across selected devices. IOSXEConfigRevision records resolved-intent history for rollback and audit. IOSXEConfigApplyLog records apply attempts, family outcomes, and diff metadata without making the main status object unbounded.

Use the generated family reference when building configuration payloads: Family Reference.

docs.title: Diagnostics and Telemetry
docs.text:
Beta

IOSXEDiagnostic and IOSXETelemetry are Beta (v1alpha1). Diagnostic command output and telemetry subscription schemas may change between releases.

IOSXEDiagnostic runs read-only IOS-XE commands. It can run once, on a schedule, or inside a maintenance window. Output can stay inline or spill to ConfigMaps for larger captures.

IOSXETelemetry declares gNMI Subscribe streams and maps notifications into OpenTelemetry metrics and logs. Use it for streaming MDT from a device through the per-device VK. See Telemetry and Telemetry Cardinality.

docs.title: Operation CRDs
docs.text:
Beta

All operation CRDs are Beta (v1alpha1). DeviceOperation is the most mature surface. IOSXEOperationalAction and IOSXESoftwareUpgrade require explicit runtime gates and carry higher operational risk. See gNOI and Software Lifecycle for prerequisites and safety guidance.

Operation CRDs are separated by trust level. DeviceOperation and IOSXEDiagnostic are read-only. IOSXEOperationalAction and IOSXESoftwareUpgrade require explicit runtime enablement and should receive separate RBAC grants.

Trust level CRDs Notes Read-only DeviceOperation, IOSXEDiagnostic Safe for diagnostics and lower-trust automation when namespace RBAC is scoped appropriately. Upgrade IOSXESoftwareUpgrade Requires gnoi.enableSoftwareUpgrade or CISCO_VK_ENABLE_IOSXE_SOFTWARE_UPGRADE. Break-glass/write-class IOSXEOperationalAction Requires gnoi.enableWriteClass or CISCO_VK_ENABLE_WRITE_CLASS_GNOI.

docs.title: DeviceOperation
docs.text:
DeviceOperation is the auditable asynchronous path for read-only operations. Supported kinds are ShowCommand, ConfigDiff, PacketCapture, GNOIPing, GNOITraceroute, GNOITime, GNOIFileGet, GNOIFileStat, GNOICertGet, GNOICanGenerateCSR, GNOIRebootStatus, and GNOIOSVerify.

apiVersion: ops.cisco.vk/v1alpha1
kind: DeviceOperation
metadata:
  name: cat9300-4-gnoi-time
spec:
  deviceRef:
    name: cat9300-4
  operation:
    kind: GNOITime
  ttlSecondsAfterFinished: 600

Use GNOICertGet to test TLS and authentication before provisioning. GNOIOSVerify succeeds only after IOS-XE reports its gNXI state as Provisioned; before that, the exact not-provisioned response is a safe, read-only signal that authentication reached the OS service. System RPCs such as GNOITime are not implemented on every platform.

docs.title: IOSXEOperationalAction
docs.text:
IOSXEOperationalAction is for write-class one-shot gNOI actions. It supports Reboot, CancelReboot, KillProcess, FilePut, FileRemove, and FactoryReset, plus ProvisionCertificate for the explicit secure-gNOI bootstrap.

Every action requires spec.confirm to equal the target device name, the spec is immutable after creation, and a Running action is not dispatched a second time after controller restart. Actions and software upgrades share one platform-neutral disruptive-mutation Lease for the target device; ambiguous post-invocation outcomes are quarantined rather than overlapped.

ProvisionCertificate requires a provisionCertificate args block with the configured certificate ID and the lowercase SHA-256 of the exact tls.crt bytes followed by the exact ca.crt bytes. The worker rejects a stale intent before device access. It is gated, create-only, and separate from the read-only GNOIOSVerify operation. See the canonical provisioning workflow for its prerequisites and cleanup steps.

apiVersion: ops.cisco.vk/v1alpha1
kind: IOSXEOperationalAction
metadata:
  name: cat9300-4-reload
spec:
  deviceRef:
    name: cat9300-4
  confirm: cat9300-4
  action:
    kind: Reboot
    reboot:
      method: COLD
      delaySeconds: 0
      message: "maintenance reload"

docs.title: IOSXESoftwareUpgrade
docs.text:
IOSXESoftwareUpgrade drives the gNOI software-upgrade lifecycle. Select exactly one source intent:

  • url with sha256, or configMapRef: CVK resolves and hashes the content, then streams its bytes with gNOI OS.Install.
  • preinstalled: {}: activate one exact, activatable native inventory version without transferring or registering content.
  • deviceFile with path and sha256: verify an IOS-XE-resident file through gNOI File.Get, register it with the IOS-XE RESTCONF install RPC, and then activate its exact inventory version.
  • localPath with optional localPathSHA256: deprecated inventory-only form. It never registers the path; use deviceFile for that workflow.

Device-file registration is IOS-XE and RESTCONF only, with no CLI fallback. Unsupported capabilities, ambiguous versions, and non-activatable inventory states fail closed. ISSU is currently rejected because CVK cannot yet verify that IOS-XE selected a non-disruptive path. NoReboot normally terminates as StagedForNextBoot while the old version remains active; it does not claim a completed upgrade. PrepareOnly never calls OS.Activate; after exact native inventory and unchanged-running-version verification it terminates as Prepared with an immutable status.preparedReceipt. The provider queue blocks direct upgrades for the same device, while the rollout manager also blocks competing campaigns for the same Device UID. A completed PrepareOnly rollout may receive one append-only spec.activationApproval naming the exact plan, every target receipt, approver and UTC claim window. The manager then creates separate preinstalled activation leaves under fresh reservations; the prepared leaves remain immutable. IOS-XE individual-supervisor upgrades install active then standby and activate standby then active, with durable milestones and no automatic rollback when a safe per-supervisor rollback sequence cannot be proven.

apiVersion: ops.cisco.vk/v1alpha1
kind: IOSXESoftwareUpgrade
metadata:
  name: cat9300-4-to-17-18
spec:
  deviceRef:
    name: cat9300-4
  targetVersion: 17.18.02
  strategy: Reload
  rollbackOnFailure: true
  imageSource:
    deviceFile:
      path: flash:cat9k_iosxe.17.18.02.SPA.bin
      sha256: 8f1b9e2d1d9b6d0e000000000000000000000000000000000000000000000000
  installTimeoutSeconds: 3600
  rebootTimeoutSeconds: 1800

Staging, activation, and rollback requests are recorded before their device-mutating RPCs and are not replayed after an ambiguous result. This at-most-once policy can require operator inspection when the controller cannot determine whether IOS-XE received a recorded request.

status.executionModel: AtMostOnceV1 identifies objects managed under this safety contract. On controller upgrade, unmarked Pending and Resolving objects are adopted; later unmarked phases fail closed with LegacyStateOutcomeUnknown. Deprecated resumePolicy, maxRetries, and retryCount fields remain on the wire for compatibility but are ignored by the current reconciler; admission retains the old Retry and 3 defaults for controller rollback compatibility. Cancelled remains a recognized terminal phase for stored objects. Unknown non-empty execution-model values remain storable for downgrade safety; an older controller preserves that status, fences the device, and issues no device RPC. Any future controller that introduces a mutation-capable phase must also bump the execution-model value so older controllers can fence the unfamiliar state. For one release, the shared mutation guard lists both upgrade and operational action CRDs before either controller claims a device Lease, deterministically fencing legacy in-flight or recently invoked work even if its controller is disabled. Scan/RBAC failures block mutation, and the fixed IOS-XE compatibility window is independent of other drivers' Lease settings.

For the full operational model, see gNOI and Software Lifecycle and the Operations Runbook.

docs.title: IOSXESoftwareRollout
docs.text:
IOSXESoftwareRollout coordinates a campaign across selected IOS-XE devices. The manager freezes the plan, checks approval and policy, reserves device and topology-domain capacity, and creates immutable per-device IOSXESoftwareUpgrade leaves. Workers execute those leaves; the manager does not open device sessions.

The controller is enabled only when managed topology and the software-upgrade mutation gate are enabled and gNOI is not globally disabled. Managed topology also requires leader election, the administrator policy ConfigMap and the native admission/RBAC contract. This is a controlled-evaluation workflow: drain, staged activation, recovery and rollback have additional qualification limits. Installing the CRD alone does not authorize software mutation.

Use the managed-topology setup and software campaign workflow for prerequisites, a complete manifest, plan approval and the documented scope. Staged activation, network-evidence and recovery extensions are introduced in v2026.11.1; upgrade October v2026.10.0 installations with the matching CRDs, admission policies, chart, manager and workers before using them.

docs.title: Safety and RBAC Notes
docs.text:
Keep the read and write surfaces distinct:

  • Grant DeviceOperation and IOSXEDiagnostic to read-only automation.
  • Grant IOSXESoftwareUpgrade only to upgrade operators.
  • Grant IOSXEOperationalAction only to break-glass or tightly controlled maintenance namespaces.
  • Keep gnoi.enableWriteClass and gnoi.enableSoftwareUpgrade disabled by default in Helm values until the device, RBAC, and maintenance workflow are ready.

For live debugging, start with:

kubectl get cvk,iosxecfg,devop,xeop,xeupgrade -A
kubectl describe cvk <device-name>
kubectl logs deploy/<device-name>-vk --tail=200
kubectl get events --sort-by=.lastTimestamp

docs.title: Opt-in device actions
docs.text:
Use this guide to authorize and inspect a one-shot device mutation. It is for operators responsible for IOS-XE maintenance, with namespace-scoped write permissions and a tested device recovery path. A completed action records what was invoked and its outcome; reboot or factory-reset acceptance still requires independent convergence checks.

For a complete operating-system change, follow the IOS-XE upgrade and downgrade runbook. The software API details below supplement that procedure. For read-only requests, use Device diagnostics.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
• A working IOS-XE CiscoDevice, per-device worker, current mutation CRDs and secure gNOI connection. The request and target device must share a namespace.
  • A maintenance window, out-of-band recovery access and authorization for the specific action. Validate the workflow on a non-production device first.
  • aggregator.enabled=false: neither mutation controller runs in aggregator mode. Direct IOSXEOperationalAction requests also require the standalone topology; the chart rejects gnoi.enableWriteClass=true when topology.enabled=true. Managed topology admits campaign-owned software upgrade leaves through its separate maintenance protocol.

docs.title: RBAC and runtime gates
docs.text:
Both mutation APIs are Beta (v1alpha1) and disabled by default. Keep diagnostic permissions separate from permissions to create iosxeoperationalactions or iosxesoftwareupgrades in the ops.cisco.vk API group.

Creating an action grants broad device authority

Kubernetes RBAC cannot distinguish spec.action.kind. Permission to create IOSXEOperationalAction includes reboot, file mutation and factory-reset requests. When a signer is configured, it also includes ProvisionCertificate and therefore PKI replacement authority. Namespace RBAC is not an action-kind allowlist; restrict the principals that receive it and any additional admission controls before enabling the gate.

For an existing standalone installation, review these settings in your Helm values, preserving the rest of the installation's configuration:

aggregator:
  enabled: false
topology:
  enabled: false
gnoi:
  disabled: false
  enableWriteClass: true
  enableSoftwareUpgrade: false

Apply them through the installation-maintenance procedure, using the same release, namespace and immutable chart version. Do not disable managed topology merely to copy this example. The write-class runtime flag is --enable-write-class-gnoi; its environment equivalent is CISCO_VK_ENABLE_WRITE_CLASS_GNOI=1.

Software maintenance has a separate gnoi.enableSoftwareUpgrade gate (--enable-iosxesoftwareupgrade or CISCO_VK_ENABLE_IOSXE_SOFTWARE_UPGRADE=1). Follow the OS runbook to enable only the gate that task needs. Chart-level gates affect the applicable workers in the release; they do not authorize individual operators or operations.

Enabling either mutation gate makes IOS-XE worker Deployments use Recreate to prevent overlapping generations from sharing one at-most-once mutation identity. Allow for a brief management interruption. Disabling both gates (or all gNOI) does not immediately guarantee RollingUpdate: old mutation workers and signer cleanup must settle, and managed topology or mounted device trust can independently require Recreate.

docs.title: Run an action
docs.text:
IOSXEOperationalAction supports Reboot, CancelReboot, KillProcess, FilePut, FileRemove, FactoryReset and ProvisionCertificate. Each request has one deviceRef, spec.confirm equal to that device name, and exactly the argument block matching spec.action.kind. The spec is immutable after create.

This example requests an immediate cold reboot of default/cat9k-smoke. Only create it after completing the prerequisites and enabling the write-class gate. Save it as reload-cat9k-smoke.yaml, replacing both device references and the namespace with the authorized target:

apiVersion: ops.cisco.vk/v1alpha1
kind: IOSXEOperationalAction
metadata:
  name: reload-cat9k-smoke
  namespace: default
spec:
  deviceRef:
    name: cat9k-smoke
  confirm: cat9k-smoke
  action:
    kind: Reboot
    reboot:
      method: COLD
      delaySeconds: 0
      message: "maintenance reload"

kubectl create -f reload-cat9k-smoke.yaml
kubectl -n default get iosxeoperationalaction reload-cat9k-smoke -w

Stop the watch at a terminal phase, then inspect the status and the device. Do not create another action simply because the worker restarted or the device became temporarily unreachable.

For ProvisionCertificate, the provisionCertificate block must contain the configured certificateID and publicMaterialSHA256: lowercase SHA-256 of the exact tls.crt bytes followed by the exact ca.crt bytes. Stale IDs or digests are rejected before connecting. This action is the only path that installs the configured gNOI identity; GNOIOSVerify remains read-only. Use the certificate provisioning workflow for signer setup and cleanup. Treat factory reset as the last capability to exercise in a rollout; RBAC alone cannot selectively disable that action kind.

docs.title: Invocation and recovery
docs.text:
An action is validated in Pending and recorded as Running before the RPC. A Running action is never dispatched again. Terminal phases are Succeeded, Failed and Rejected; normal events describe running/successful requests, and warning events describe rejection, failure or pending deletion.

After a controller restart, CVK waits for the original five-minute RPC window and a short persistence grace. Without a durably recorded result, the action fails with ActionOutcomeUnknown and its Lease stays quarantined until expiry. Inspect the device before creating a replacement request.

For certificate provisioning, CertificateInstallIndeterminate means the create-only result remained unknown after bounded certificate and OS.Verify checks over fresh connections. Use GNOICertGet and inspect device PKI state; never blindly retry the same certificate ID.

docs.title: IOSXEOperationalAction — example output
docs.text:
kubectl -n default get iosxeoperationalaction reload-cat9k-smoke -o yaml
kubectl -n default describe iosxeoperationalaction reload-cat9k-smoke

An accepted reboot can have the following abbreviated status:

status:
  phase: Succeeded
  invocationID: "a3f2e1d0-8c7b-4a5f-9e6d-1b2c3d4e5f60"
  conditions:
    - type: Ready
      status: "True"
      reason: AcceptedPendingConvergence

For Reboot and FactoryReset, this means the device accepted the RPC. It does not establish recovery or convergence, and the mutation Lease remains quarantined until expiry. Verify reachability and resulting device state independently before declaring maintenance complete.

docs.title: Shared device-mutation Lease
docs.text:
Actions and software upgrades share a platform-neutral device-disruptive-mutation Lease for each namespaced device. Its safety TTL is 26 hours in this release. Definitive outcomes release the Lease; every invoked action failure, accepted reboot/factory reset, and uncertain upgrade outcome retains it until expiry. Delayed reboots add their accepted delay to the hold. CancelReboot bypasses coordination and never releases another holder's Lease.

An in-flight action retains its finalizer through the bounded RPC and persistence window. If its outcome remains unknown, CVK records ActionOutcomeUnknown, allows deletion to complete and retains quarantine. Deleting a software-upgrade CR does not cancel device work or clear a required quarantine. Disabling a gate also does not discard an existing quarantine.

The fence identifies a device by namespace and CiscoDevice name, not its IP. Register a physical device once and coordinate ownership across clusters. Manual CLI and external automation remain outside this fence. See gNOI mutation coordination for the maintenance taint, app-hosting/configuration-write guard and managed campaign behavior.

docs.title: Software upgrade API details
docs.text: Use the OS upgrade and downgrade runbook for the complete procedure, credentials, recovery prerequisites and verification. This reference retains the source-selection, strategy and compatibility contracts needed to interpret IOSXESoftwareUpgrade objects.

docs.title: Image sources
docs.text:
Select exactly one source in spec.imageSource:

Source Behavior and constraint url with sha256 Fetch and verify the content, then stream it through gNOI OS.Install. configMapRef Stream binaryData["image"] through OS.Install; the roughly 900 KiB ConfigMap limit makes this a testing-only source. preinstalled: {} Activate an exact native-inventory version without transfer or registration. deviceFile with path and sha256 Verify through gNOI File.Get, register through IOS-XE RESTCONF install, then activate through gNOI. Deprecated localPath, optionally localPathSHA256 Inventory-only compatibility form; never registers a file.

Device-file registration has no CLI fallback. Ambiguous or non-activatable inventory fails closed. URL credentials must not appear as URL user information. For FTP/SCP/SFTP, an optional same-namespace urlSecretRef must have label cisco.vk/purpose=software-image-source and keys allowedScheme, allowedHost and allowedPort matching the canonical endpoint before credentials are loaded. See the Secret and transfer contract.

docs.title: Strategies, preparation and rollback
docs.text:
Strategy Current behavior Reload (default) Activates the selected image and reloads the device. ISSU Rejected during preflight until CVK can verify IOS-XE selected the ISSU path. NoReboot Requests activation without immediate reload; if the old version remains running, ends as StagedForNextBoot and needs a separately authorized reboot. It is not a hitless-upgrade guarantee. PrepareOnly Accepts URL, ConfigMap or deviceFile sources, never calls OS.Activate, verifies the old version remains running, and ends as Prepared with an immutable content-addressed receipt.

A retained preparation receipt blocks both direct upgrades for the same device and a competing managed campaign for the same Device UID. For managed activation, the completed rollout needs append-only spec.activationApproval, the exact frozen plan and receipt set, a bounded UTC window and the distinct activate permission. CVK creates a new preinstalled activation leaf and reservation, then revalidates inventory, trust, source, policy, identity, health and workload safety before claiming activation. The prepared leaf remains audit evidence; deleting it is never an authorization workflow. Follow separate preparation and activation for that approval procedure.

When OS.Verify requires individual-supervisor handling, CVK installs active then standby, activates standby then active, rejects NoReboot, and uses one shared install deadline.

With rollbackOnFailure: true, a different running version after activation can enter RollingBack only if the previous version was captured and the backend proves it remains activatable. RolledBack requires OS.Verify to confirm that version. Automatic rollback is rejected for individual-supervisor handling because a safe, separately verified sequence for both supervisors is not yet established.

Staging, activation and rollback intent is persisted before its RPC and is not replayed after an ambiguous result. Inspect the device when an outcome remains unknown; submitting a replacement is a new maintenance decision.

docs.title: IOSXESoftwareUpgrade — example output
docs.text:
For an upgrade created through the OS runbook, substitute its actual namespace and name:

kubectl -n edge get iosxesoftwareupgrade cat9000-1-to-17-18-03 -w
kubectl -n edge describe iosxesoftwareupgrade cat9000-1-to-17-18-03

A successful transfer/reload can progress through Pending → Resolving → Transferring → Activating → AwaitingReachability → Verifying → Succeeded. A deviceFile source uses Staging and Validating before activation. Inspect the pinned source digest, staging operation ID, inventory, conditions and events; terminal preparation or staging is not proof that the target version is running.

docs.title: Migrating existing mutation objects
docs.text:
The current at-most-once reconciler adopts an unmarked legacy upgrade only in Pending or Resolving. A later unmarked phase may already have submitted a mutation, so it ends with LegacyStateOutcomeUnknown and a quarantined Lease. Inspect device state before replacing it.

Older manifests may retain resumePolicy and maxRetries; stored status may retain retryCount or phase Cancelled. Admission preserves the historical Retry and 3 defaults for controller rollback compatibility, but the current reconciler ignores those retry fields. An unknown non-empty execution-model marker is preserved as newer-controller state: CVK holds the Lease and issues no RPC rather than rewriting or replaying the operation.

During this migration, either mutation controller reads both mutation CRDs before claiming a Lease, including when the other controller is disabled. It chooses a deterministic legacy quarantine holder and fails closed on API or RBAC errors. Released invoked actions retain a bounded 26-hour safety window plus any accepted reboot delay, independent of future drivers' normal Lease settings.

docs.title: Device diagnostics
docs.text: Use DeviceOperation to collect auditable, asynchronous diagnostic results without creating a Pod or changing device state. This guide is for operators with permission to inspect a device and create read-only operations. The expected result is a terminal operation with output, artifact references or a specific failure reason.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
• A working CiscoDevice and its per-device worker, with the current DeviceOperation CRD installed. Examples use the IOS-XE device default/cat9k-smoke; replace both namespace and name together.
  • Namespace-scoped permission to create and inspect DeviceOperation objects. The operation must be in the same namespace as its target device; cross-namespace requests are rejected with NamespaceMismatch.
  • The device transport and credentials needed for the selected operation. gNOI probes additionally need gNOI enabled and a working secure connection; RPC availability depends on the device and software version. See gNOI and software lifecycle for that setup.

The API is Beta (v1alpha1). Leave write-class and software-upgrade gates off for read-only use; these diagnostics do not require either mutation gate.

docs.title: Run a read-only operation
docs.text:
Save this as show-version.yaml, substituting your existing device and namespace:

apiVersion: ops.cisco.vk/v1alpha1
kind: DeviceOperation
metadata:
  name: show-version
  namespace: default
spec:
  deviceRef:
    name: cat9k-smoke
  operation:
    kind: ShowCommand
    commands:
      - show version
  ttlSecondsAfterFinished: 300

kubectl apply -f show-version.yaml
kubectl -n default get deviceoperation show-version -w

When it reaches a terminal phase, stop the watch and inspect its output and events. The example requests cleanup five minutes after completion, so collect needed evidence before then. Use a new operation name for a later probe to keep its audit record separate.

docs.title: Supported read-only kinds
docs.text:
Kind What it reads Request details ShowCommand Allowlisted IOS-XE show/monitor commands operation.commands; the allowlist is shared with IOSXEDiagnostic. ConfigDiff show running-config, optionally compared with a baseline Optional operation.args.baseline produces a compact line diff. PacketCapture An existing IOS-XE capture buffer operation.args.name or operation.args.capture. GNOIPing Reachability from the device (System service) Typed operation.gnoi.ping arguments. GNOITraceroute Hop-by-hop path from the device (System) Typed operation.gnoi.traceroute arguments. GNOITime Device clock (System) No mutation. GNOIFileGet Bounded file content (File) Preview or ConfigMap artifact. GNOIFileStat File metadata (File) Inspect a staged file. GNOICertGet Installed certificates (Cert) Check secure-gNXI connectivity before provisioning. GNOICanGenerateCSR CSR capability (Cert) Check a key/certificate profile. GNOIRebootStatus Pending or active reboot state (System) Observe an existing request. GNOIOSVerify Running version and activation state (OS) Requires IOS-XE OS-service provisioning for success.

GNOIOSVerify never provisions or changes the device. Before IOS-XE reports State: Provisioned, its expected not-provisioned response can confirm that authentication reached the OS service. Successful TLS/password authentication does not prove every System or File RPC is supported. For certificate setup, follow the provisioning procedure.

docs.title: Restrict ConfigDiff
docs.text:
Running configurations can contain sensitive data. A platform operator can restrict ConfigDiff using CiscoDevice.spec.opsPolicy.configDiffAllowedNamespaces. For an existing device in default, this patch allows ConfigDiff in default:

kubectl -n default patch ciscodevice cat9k-smoke --type=merge \
  -p '{"spec":{"opsPolicy":{"configDiffAllowedNamespaces":["default"]}}}'

This list is an additional restriction, not permission to target a device from another namespace. An empty or absent list adds no ConfigDiff-specific restriction, but the same-namespace rule and Kubernetes RBAC still apply. Requests denied by the list have Ready=False, reason NamespaceNotAuthorized.

The controller renders the list as CVK_OPS_CONFIGDIFF_ALLOWED_NAMESPACES on the worker. Change the CiscoDevice spec; imperative kubectl set env edits are reverted during reconciliation.

docs.title: Read a capture buffer
docs.text:
PacketCapture synthesizes only show monitor capture <name> buffer dump. It does not start a capture. The former operation.args.command escape hatch has been removed; use ShowCommand with explicit commands for other allowlisted show or monitor commands.

For example, the operation portion of a request for an existing buffer is:

operation:
  kind: PacketCapture
  args:
    name: capture1

Capture output over 256 KiB is stored in a ConfigMap in the operation's namespace. Standalone workers use <deviceoperation-name>-output; managed topology uses an identity-bound generated name. Read the actual reference from status, which retains a truncated inline preview and an artifact URI such as configmap://default/capture-output/output. Captures over 900 KiB fail with Ready=False, reason ArtifactTooLarge; use a smaller existing buffer rather than assuming output was retained.

docs.title: Status
docs.text: Inspect .status.phase, .status.conditions, .status.outputs[] and .status.artifactURIs[]. Terminal phases are Succeeded, Failed and Cancelled. ttlSecondsAfterFinished requests best-effort cleanup after completion; absent or zero disables that cleanup. Export needed evidence before a TTL removes the operation and its owned artifacts.

docs.title: DeviceOperation — example output
docs.text:
kubectl -n default get deviceoperation show-version -o yaml
kubectl -n default describe deviceoperation show-version

A successful show-command request has a status shaped like this (output is abbreviated; actual device text varies):

status:
  phase: Succeeded
  conditions:
    - type: Ready
      status: "True"
      reason: Succeeded
  outputs:
    - command: show version
      output: "Cisco IOS XE Software, Version ..."

Events record dispatch and completion. A GNOIPing result uses the same output path and includes probe replies and sent/received/latency statistics. For a failed probe, read the condition message and events before retrying; a transport or unsupported-RPC failure is different from evidence that the target is down.

docs.title: RBAC
docs.text:
Give diagnostic operators their own namespace-scoped permissions on deviceoperations.ops.cisco.vk. Artifact readers also need permission to read the referenced ConfigMaps. Keep these grants separate from IOSXEOperationalAction and software-upgrade authority.

The per-device worker service account watches operations targeting its device. Its create permission supports the local admin wrapper, and delete supports TTL cleanup; result writes use deviceoperations/status. These worker grants do not replace the operator's own authorization.

docs.title: Admin exec wrapper
docs.text: When its in-pod controller client is available, the local admin endpoint POST /v1/exec creates a transient DeviceOperation and polls status. This preserves the plugin response shape while routing execution through the CRD audit path.

docs.title: Implementation boundary
docs.text: Read-only kinds share validation, transport, redaction, bounded output, TTL and status handling. Mutating actions use a separate reconciler and CRD with their own RBAC, confirmation guard, finalizer, invocation ID, events and at-most-once dispatch rules. See device actions before enabling them.

docs.title: Roadmap gates
docs.text: The current boundaries remain explicit: broader write-class use needs tenant ownership/admission controls; API promotion beyond v1alpha1 needs conversion handling; large diagnostic artifacts currently use in-namespace ConfigMaps; and automatic rollback does not cover cross-device or independently verified multi-supervisor recovery. These are not capabilities implied by a successful read-only probe.

docs.title: Environment Variables Support
docs.text: The Cisco Virtual Kubelet provider supports Kubernetes environment variables in container specifications, allowing applications to receive configuration data from multiple sources. This document describes the supported environment variable types, limitations, and best practices.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text: Environment variables are passed to containers running on IOS-XE devices via Docker -e flags in the RunOpts configuration. Supported sources are explicit env values, secretKeyRef and configMapKeyRef. fieldRef and resourceFieldRef return an error; envFrom is not expanded. Empty resolved values are omitted. This page describes IOS-XE; NX-OS has different value restrictions.

docs.title: ✅ Direct Values
docs.text:
Static key-value pairs defined directly in the container specification:

env:
  - name: NODE_ENV
    value: "production"
  - name: PORT
    value: "8080"
  - name: DEBUG_MODE
    value: "false"

docs.title: ✅ Secret References
docs.text:
Values resolved from Kubernetes Secrets for sensitive data:

env:
  - name: DB_PASSWORD
    valueFrom:
      secretKeyRef:
        name: database-credentials
        key: password
  - name: API_TOKEN
    valueFrom:
      secretKeyRef:
        name: api-secrets
        key: token
        optional: true  # Won't fail if secret/key is missing

docs.title: ✅ ConfigMap References
docs.text:
Values resolved from Kubernetes ConfigMaps for configuration data:

env:
  - name: API_BASE_URL
    valueFrom:
      configMapKeyRef:
        name: app-config
        key: api-url
  - name: LOG_LEVEL
    valueFrom:
      configMapKeyRef:
        name: app-config
        key: log-level
        optional: true

docs.title: RunOpts Character Limits
docs.text:
IOS-XE App-Hosting has specific limitations for Docker RunOpts configuration:

  • Maximum Lines: 30 lines
  • Maximum Characters Per Line: 235, counted as bytes by the current implementation
  • Gross Capacity: 30 × 235 bytes, shared with labels, hostname, option names and quoting

The provider distributes complete options across lines; it never splits one option. A single oversized option or a need for more than 30 lines fails Pod configuration rather than truncating a value. The gross capacity is not a 7,050-byte allowance for environment values alone.

docs.title: Security Features
docs.text:
• Portable names: Names must match [A-Za-z_][A-Za-z0-9_]*.
  • Value wrapping: Values are wrapped in single quotes; embedded single quotes are escaped by closing and reopening the quoted string.
  • Literal special characters: Dollar signs, backticks and double quotes remain literal inside the single-quoted value.

Secret values become device app-hosting run options and can be read by device administrators. CVK does not include resolved options in its diagnostic logs; see Hosted-application credentials.

docs.title: Required Resources
docs.text:
If a required Secret or ConfigMap is missing, pod deployment will fail with a descriptive error:

failed to resolve environment variable DB_PASSWORD: failed to get secret db-credentials: secret not found

docs.title: Optional Resources
docs.text: If an optional Secret or ConfigMap is missing (marked with optional: true), the environment variable is silently omitted and deployment continues.

docs.title: Missing Keys
docs.text: If a required key is missing from an existing Secret/ConfigMap, deployment fails. Optional keys are silently omitted.

docs.title: Security
docs.text:
1. Use Secrets for sensitive data: Passwords, API keys, tokens
  2. Use ConfigMaps for configuration: URLs, timeouts, feature flags
  3. Mark appropriate resources as optional: Non-critical configuration
  4. Avoid embedding secrets in direct values: Use Secret references instead

docs.title: Performance
docs.text:
1. Minimize total environment variable size: Leave room for option syntax, labels and hostname within the RunOpts limits
  2. Use short variable names: Reduces RunOpts overhead
  3. Consolidate configuration: Group related settings in ConfigMaps

docs.title: Organization
docs.text:
1. Use descriptive Secret/ConfigMap names: database-credentials, app-config
  2. Use consistent naming conventions: DB_PASSWORD, API_BASE_URL
  3. Document required vs optional variables: In pod annotations or README

docs.title: Complete Pod with Mixed Sources
docs.text:
Create the production namespace first and register the intended virtual Node. This example targets cat9000-1 and assumes a signed application package is already at flash:/web-app.iosxe.tar on that device. Change those values for your setup; a registry reference such as nginx:latest is not a device image. See Image delivery.

apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
  name: web-app
  namespace: production
spec:
  nodeName: cat9000-1
  tolerations:
  - key: virtual-kubelet.io/provider
    operator: Exists
  containers:
  - name: web-server
    image: flash:/web-app.iosxe.tar
    env:
    # Direct configuration
    - name: NODE_ENV
      value: "production"
    - name: PORT
      value: "8080"

    # Database credentials from secret
    - name: DB_HOST
      valueFrom:
        configMapKeyRef:
          name: database-config
          key: host
    - name: DB_PASSWORD
      valueFrom:
        secretKeyRef:
          name: database-credentials
          key: password

    # Optional features
    - name: ANALYTICS_API_KEY
      valueFrom:
        secretKeyRef:
          name: analytics-keys
          key: api-key
          optional: true

    # Application configuration
    - name: API_BASE_URL
      valueFrom:
        configMapKeyRef:
          name: app-config
          key: api-url
    - name: CACHE_TTL
      valueFrom:
        configMapKeyRef:
          name: app-config
          key: cache-ttl
          optional: true
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: Secret
metadata:
  name: database-credentials
  namespace: production
type: Opaque
stringData:
  password: <application-password>
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: ConfigMap
metadata:
  name: app-config
  namespace: production
data:
  api-url: "https://api.example.com/v1"
  cache-ttl: "300"
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: ConfigMap
metadata:
  name: database-config
  namespace: production
data:
  host: "db.production.example.com"
  port: "5432"

docs.title: Generated Docker Command
docs.text:
CVK configures IOS-XE RunOpts rather than invoking a local docker run. The environment portion contains options like these, packed with the labels and hostname into the available lines (the password is redacted here):

-e NODE_ENV='production'
-e PORT='8080'
-e DB_HOST='db.production.example.com'
-e DB_PASSWORD='<resolved password>'
-e API_BASE_URL='https://api.example.com/v1'
-e CACHE_TTL='300'

Note: ANALYTICS_API_KEY is omitted because the optional secret doesn't exist.

docs.title: Pod Deployment Fails
docs.text:
1. Check Secret/ConfigMap existence: kubectl get secret,configmap -n <namespace>
  2. Verify key names: Describe the Secret or ConfigMap in the Pod's namespace; avoid sharing secret values in diagnostic output
  3. Check namespaces: Resources must be in the same namespace as the pod
  4. Review error messages: Pod events contain specific error details

docs.title: Environment Variables Missing in Container
docs.text:
1. Verify resolution worked: Check pod events for resolution errors
  2. Check optional vs required: Optional missing resources are silently omitted
  3. Check empty values: Empty direct or resolved values are omitted by the current implementation
  4. Test with direct values: Isolate whether the issue is with resolution or container setup

docs.title: Character Limit Exceeded
docs.text:
Inspect the Pod Events and worker error for either single RunOpts option too long or too many RunOpts lines needed. Counting YAML characters does not measure the rendered options: referenced values, quoting, labels and hostname all affect the result. Errors report sizes without printing resolved secrets.

If approaching limits:

  1. Use shorter variable names
  2. Consolidate related configuration into fewer variables
  3. Use the application's supported configuration delivery for large files, such as packaging non-secret configuration with the app or fetching it through an authenticated application mechanism; generic ConfigMap volume projection is not provided by this RunOpts path
  4. Split functionality only when the application supports separate containers, each with its own bounded options

docs.title: Generated Configuration
docs.text:
Environment variables are integrated into IOS-XE App-Hosting configuration. The provider enables docker-resource mode with prepend-pkg-opts and sets the container hostname to the container name. This excerpt illustrates the shape; actual app IDs use cvk<index>_<pod-uid> and line packing depends on the complete options:

app-hosting appid cvk00000_<pod-uid>
 app-vnic management guest-interface 0
 app-default-gateway 192.168.1.1 guest-interface 0
 app-resource docker
  prepend-pkg-opts
  run-opts 1 "--label pod=web-app --hostname=web-server -e NODE_ENV='production'"
  run-opts 2 "-e DB_PASSWORD='<resolved password>'"
 app-resource profile custom
  cpu 1000
  memory 512
  • prepend-pkg-opts: Ensures Docker run options are prepended to the container command.
  • --hostname=<container-name>: Sets the container hostname to the Kubernetes container name from the pod spec.

docs.title: Monitoring
docs.text:
Check app status and environment variable propagation:

# On IOS-XE device
show app-hosting list
show app-hosting detail appid <app-id>
show app-hosting utilization appid <app-id>

Use the application's own diagnostic or logging mechanism to verify received settings without printing secrets. Kubernetes logs, exec, attach and port-forward are unsupported for hosted applications; worker Pod logs show CVK lifecycle and resolution errors. See application diagnostics.

docs.title: CVK netascode family parity
docs.text:

docs.title: Getting Started
docs.text:
This guide walks you through deploying Cisco Virtual Kubelet against a Kubernetes cluster and running your first pod on a Cisco IOS-XE device.

You'll install the Helm chart, which deploys a Kubernetes controller. The controller watches CiscoDevice custom resources and stands up a Virtual Kubelet pod for each one — this is the supported way to run Cisco Virtual Kubelet.

NX-OS (Beta)

This walkthrough uses an IOS-XE device, the production-focused path. Cisco Nexus (NX-OS) switches are also supported in Beta — the install and pod workflow is the same, with platform-specific device settings, credentials, node name and package path. See the substitutions in Deploying to NX-OS below and the NX-OS Family Reference.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
Requirement Notes Kubernetes cluster v1.28+ recommended Helm 3.21+ or 4.2+ For installing the chart Docker (or compatible) Optional; only needed to build a custom VK image Container registry Optional for custom images; the published image is on GHCR Cisco IOS-XE device Catalyst 8000V (17.15.4c+), Catalyst 9000 (17.18.2+), IR1100 Series (17.12.4+), or IE3500 Series (17.18.2+) kubectl Configured to talk to your cluster

On the device you need:

  • iox configured — Cisco's on-device container runtime.
  • restconf enabled on the HTTPS listener.
  • App-hosting support (standard on Catalyst 8000V and 9000).
  • A signed container tar on device flash (e.g. flash:/hello-app.iosxe.tar on Cat8000V/Cat9000/IE3500, or bootflash:/hello-app.iosxe.tar on IR1100) unless you explicitly allow unsigned packages.

See the platform-specific install guide for the exact IOS-XE CLI snippets: Catalyst 8000V, Catalyst 9000, IR1100 Series, or IE3500 Series.

docs.title: 1. Install the controller
docs.text:
The controller watches CiscoDevice custom resources and creates a Virtual Kubelet deployment for each one.

The release chart needs no source checkout, image build, or private registry. These commands target November v2026.11.1; run them only after that version and its artifacts appear on the Releases page. If it is not listed, use the published October 2026.10.0 chart with its matching documentation. Do not use the rejected, unpublished v2026.11.0 artifacts. The chart selects its matching signed image automatically.

helm install cvk oci://ghcr.io/cisco-open/charts/cisco-virtual-kubelet \
  --version 2026.11.1 \
  --namespace cvk-system --create-namespace

This pulls the signed ghcr.io/cisco-open/cisco-virtual-kubelet image by default. The chart --version matches the release's SemVer-compatible CalVer without the leading v (for example, v2026.11.1 → 2026.11.1); see Releases for the current one.

The chart installs:

  • All shipped cisco.vk, config.cisco.vk, and ops.cisco.vk CRDs
  • The controller Deployment (single replica by default; leader election is opt-in)
  • RBAC for the manager and per-device VK pods

Both the controller pod and each VK pod it spawns use this image. To use different images for the two, set controllerImage.* and vkImage.* instead.

The sdwan and nexus-dashboard adapters and managed public-CA Secret projection are introduced in v2026.11.1. October installations need the full upgrade procedure before using them; applying a November example alone does not update the CRDs or running image. For local changes, see custom builds.

Verify:

kubectl -n cvk-system get pods
kubectl get crd ciscodevices.cisco.vk

If the controller pod is not Running, see Troubleshooting → CiscoDevice stuck in Provisioning.

docs.title: 2. Create a credential Secret
docs.text:
Device credentials are injected into the VK pod via a Kubernetes Secret — the controller never stores them in the ConfigMap. The Secret must be in the same namespace as the CiscoDevice and have a key named exactly password.

Save this as secret.yaml, replacing the password placeholder:

apiVersion: v1
kind: Secret
metadata:
  name: cat9000-1-creds
  namespace: default
type: Opaque
stringData:
  password: <device-password>

kubectl apply -f secret.yaml

Need multiple devices with different credentials? See Security → Managing credentials across multiple devices.

docs.title: 3. Create a CiscoDevice
docs.text:
The CiscoDevice CR describes how to reach the device and how containers should be networked on it.

Save this as ciscodevice.yaml, adapting the address, username and networking to your device:

apiVersion: cisco.vk/v1alpha1
kind: CiscoDevice
metadata:
  name: cat9000-1
  namespace: default
spec:
  driver: XE
  address: "192.168.1.100"
  port: 443
  username: admin
  credentialSecretRef:
    name: cat9000-1-creds      # matches the Secret from step 2
  tls:
    enabled: true
    insecureSkipVerify: false
  # allowUnsignedApps: true     # uncomment for unsigned packages (own builds /
                                 # test images). CVK disables device signing via
                                 # RESTCONF and relaxes the reconciler guard.
  xe:
    networking:
      interface:
        type: AppGigabitEthernet
        appGigabitEthernet:
          mode: trunk
          vlanIf:
            dhcp: true
            vlan: 200
            guestInterface: 0

This Catalyst 9000 example uses the app-hosting VLAN and DHCP setup from the platform guide. For Catalyst 8000V, use its VirtualPortGroup configuration instead. The device HTTPS certificate must be trusted by the worker's system CA store and match spec.address (an IP SAN when using an IP address). For a private CA, see the managed Secret alternative below; October deployments need a custom verified CA mount as described in Shared TLS. This quick-start configuration leaves gNOI in backward-compatible auto mode. Before invoking a gNOI operation, configure explicit verified gNOI TLS.

Private CA support introduced in v2026.11.1

spec.tls.caSecretRef requires the November CRD, admission policies, manager and workers. Upgrade those components together when moving from v2026.10.0; see the projection and rollback requirements.

Create a Secret from an independently trusted public CA bundle in the same namespace as the CiscoDevice:

kubectl -n default create secret generic switch-https-public-ca \
  --from-file=ca.crt=/path/to/trusted-device-ca.crt

Replace the device's tls block with:

tls:
  enabled: true
  insecureSkipVerify: false
  caSecretRef:
    name: switch-https-public-ca

The controller projects only validated public CA certificates. This does not install a certificate on the device or configure dedicated gNOI trust.

kubectl apply -f ciscodevice.yaml

Within a few seconds you should see:

$ kubectl get ciscodevice
NAME         DRIVER   ADDRESS         PHASE      AGE
cat9000-1    XE       192.168.1.100   Ready      15s

$ kubectl get nodes
NAME         STATUS   ROLES   AGE
cat9000-1    Ready    agent   15s

If PHASE stays on Provisioning or shows Error, see Troubleshooting.

docs.title: Deploying to NX-OS (Beta)
docs.text:
For a Cisco Nexus (NX-OS) switch, use the same controller installation in step 1. In step 2, name the credential Secret nexus9300v-01-creds in namespace default and supply that switch's password. Set driver: NXOS and use an nxos: block instead of xe:. App-hosting is driven over NX-API CLI; the only supported host-side attachment today is the Management interface.

apiVersion: cisco.vk/v1alpha1
kind: CiscoDevice
metadata:
  name: nexus9300v-01
  namespace: default
spec:
  driver: NXOS
  address: "192.168.1.120"
  port: 443
  username: admin
  credentialSecretRef:
    name: nexus9300v-01-creds
  tls:
    enabled: true
    insecureSkipVerify: false  # requires a certificate trusted by the worker
  nxos:
    networking:
      interface:
        type: Management
        management:
          guestInterface: 0

In the Pod manifest from step 4, replace spec.nodeName with nexus9300v-01 and spec.containers[0].image with the path to an NX-OS-compatible package, for example bootflash:/hello-app.nxos.tar. Stage that package on the switch first. The IOS-XE example's flash: prefix is not accepted: NX-OS accepts bootflash: paths or supported HTTP(S) package URLs. Keep the pod's namespace consistent with your credential and device examples (default).

Declarative NX-OS device configuration (VLANs, interfaces, features, and so on) is managed separately through the NXOSConfig CRD over NX-API REST/DME — see the NX-OS Family Reference for the supported families and an example. NX-OS is a Beta runtime slice; the Production Readiness page tracks its current scope.

docs.title: 4. Deploy a pod
docs.text:
Schedule a pod directly onto the virtual node.

apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
  name: hello-app
spec:
  nodeName: cat9000-1
  tolerations:
  - key: virtual-kubelet.io/provider
    operator: Exists
  containers:
  - name: hello
    image: flash:/hello-app.iosxe.tar   # path on device flash (use bootflash: on IR1100)
    resources:
      requests:
        memory: "512Mi"
        cpu: "500m"
      limits:
        memory: "1Gi"
        cpu: "1000m"

The image reference is a path on the device's flash storage, not a container registry reference — the container tar must already be on the device, or be served over HTTP(S). To serve images from a registry, see Image Distribution.

kubectl apply -f pod.yaml
kubectl get pod hello-app -w

If the pod stays in Pending for more than a minute or ends up Failed, see Troubleshooting → Pod stuck in Pending or PackagePolicyInvalid false positives.

docs.title: 5. Verify on the device
docs.text:
ssh admin@192.168.1.100
# show app-hosting list
# show app-hosting detail appid cvk00000_<pod-uid>

You should see the container transition through DEPLOYED → ACTIVATED → RUNNING. Typical output of show app-hosting list:

App id                                    State
----------------------------------------------------
cvk00000_a1b2c3d4...                      RUNNING

docs.title: Upgrading an existing release
docs.text:
Helm installs CRDs during the first install but does not upgrade them. Before upgrading to 2026.11.1, confirm publication as described above, pull that chart, and back up the live definitions and custom resources. November refreshes 18 existing CRD manifests, with substantive schema changes in four and no new kinds. Preserve reviewed Helm values, inspect the server-side diff, and apply the reviewed schemas with an explicit Helm field-ownership handoff:

helm pull oci://ghcr.io/cisco-open/charts/cisco-virtual-kubelet \
  --version 2026.11.1 --untar
kubectl get customresourcedefinitions.apiextensions.k8s.io -o yaml \
  > cvk-crds-before-upgrade.yaml
kubectl diff --server-side --force-conflicts \
  --field-manager=cvk-crd-upgrade -f cisco-virtual-kubelet/crds/
kubectl apply --server-side --force-conflicts \
  --field-manager=cvk-crd-upgrade -f cisco-virtual-kubelet/crds/
kubectl wait --for=condition=Established --timeout=60s \
  -f cisco-virtual-kubelet/crds/

helm upgrade cvk oci://ghcr.io/cisco-open/charts/cisco-virtual-kubelet \
  --version 2026.11.1 \
  --namespace cvk-system
kubectl rollout status deployment/cvk-cisco-virtual-kubelet-controller \
  --namespace cvk-system

kubectl diff returns status 1 for expected differences. The force flag is limited to the exact CVK CRD files passed with -f; review the diff and keep the backup before continuing.

The September release adds NetworkController and NetworkControllerConfig. If either CRD is absent, the manager keeps existing device reconcilers running but disables the Alpha controller scaffold for that process. Apply both CRDs and restart the manager. See Upgrading CRDs for verification and rollback guidance.

docs.title: Optional: install the kubectl plugin with Krew
docs.text:
The client-side kubectl-ciscovk plugin is optional; the controller and normal Kubernetes workflows do not depend on it. It provides read-only, ad-hoc IOS-XE commands and manager-accepted topology graph diagnostics. Graph output is observational and never grants rollout authority; optional declared mappings and links live in an admission-protected ConfigMap key separate from rollout policy hashes. It is available in the public Krew index; install and upgrade it with:

kubectl krew update
kubectl krew install cisco-vk
kubectl cisco-vk version

# Later releases
kubectl krew upgrade cisco-vk

Historical note: v2026.08.0 predates the plugin assets, and v2026.8.1 was the first plugin-bearing release. The CLI & Plugin Reference documents Krew, signed-archive, and source-build paths plus the plugin's current IOS-XE-only scope.

docs.title: Optional: build a custom image
docs.text:
Use a custom build only when you need code changes or are evaluating a development feature. For a released baseline, select an explicit tag from the published Releases page. Do not infer publication from the greatest Git tag: draft and rejected candidates can also have tags.

git clone https://github.com/cisco-open/cisco-virtual-kubelet.git
cd cisco-virtual-kubelet
VERSION=v2026.11.1  # use only after publication; otherwise select a published baseline
git checkout "$VERSION"
IMAGE_REPOSITORY=ghcr.io/your-org/cisco-vk  # replace with your registry path

docker build -t "$IMAGE_REPOSITORY:$VERSION" .
docker push "$IMAGE_REPOSITORY:$VERSION"

helm install cvk ./charts/cisco-virtual-kubelet \
  --namespace cvk-system --create-namespace \
  --set image.repository="$IMAGE_REPOSITORY" \
  --set image.tag="$VERSION"

For a development build, check out the intended commit and use a unique image tag for it; install the chart and CRDs from that same checkout. This is an evaluation deployment with its own provenance, not a release artifact. For KIND or minikube, you can load the built image locally instead of pushing it:

kind load docker-image "$IMAGE_REPOSITORY:$VERSION" --name kind
# Or:
minikube image load "$IMAGE_REPOSITORY:$VERSION"

docs.title: What's next
docs.text:
• Configuration — Every field with defaults and validation rules
  • Observability — Enable OpenTelemetry topology traces and scrape Prometheus metrics
  • Security — TLS, credential rotation, and RBAC
  • Troubleshooting — If anything above did not work

docs.title: Glossary
docs.text:
Terms used throughout the guides and reference pages. For resource fields and workflows, use the CRD reference and reference overview.

Term Meaning App-Hosting Cisco's on-device container platform. Runs .tar container packages on IOS-XE devices. CDP Cisco Discovery Protocol, used for Layer 2 neighbor discovery. CR / CRD Custom Resource / Custom Resource Definition, Kubernetes' API extension mechanism. gNMI gRPC Network Management Interface, used for model-driven telemetry and optional config transport. gNOI gRPC Network Operations Interface, used for read-only probes, file operations, reboot, factory reset, and software upgrade flows. IOx Cisco's on-device application hosting framework, including App-Hosting. Network as Code Declarative intent shape consumed by IOSXEConfig, NXOSConfig, and, with a registered adapter, controller-centric NetworkControllerConfig. OTEL / OpenTelemetry Vendor-neutral observability framework; this project emits OTEL traces and metrics. RESTCONF HTTP/JSON management API for network devices, defined by RFC 8040, modeled by YANG. Virtual Kubelet Upstream project letting any system appear as a Kubernetes node. VK Short for Virtual Kubelet. VPG / VirtualPortGroup A logical L3 interface on IOS-XE used to bridge app-hosted containers into the device network. YANG Data modeling language used to describe configuration and state.

docs.title: IOS-XE gNOI Upgrade and Downgrade Runbook
docs.text:
Beta and disruptive

IOSXESoftwareUpgrade is a Beta (v1alpha1) API. A Reload activation reboots the switch. Validate the exact image and recovery procedure in a lab, use an approved maintenance window, keep console or out-of-band access available, and upgrade one device at a time.

This is the complete operator path for upgrading and then downgrading an IOS-XE device through CVK. The detailed API, security, and failure semantics remain in gNOI and Software Lifecycle.

docs.title: The mental model
docs.text:
An upgrade and a planned downgrade are the same operation in CVK:

  1. The per-device CVK worker downloads and SHA-256 verifies the selected image.
  2. CVK streams those bytes to IOS-XE with gNOI OS.Install.
  3. CVK asks IOS-XE to activate the exact version returned by Install.
