Both write-class gNOI surfaces are opt-in on the per-device VK pod:

  • IOSXEOperationalAction requires --enable-write-class-gnoi or CISCO_VK_ENABLE_WRITE_CLASS_GNOI=true.
  • IOSXESoftwareUpgrade requires --enable-iosxesoftwareupgrade or CISCO_VK_ENABLE_IOSXE_SOFTWARE_UPGRADE=true.

For a legacy combined worker, check its args and logs:

kubectl -n <device-namespace> get deploy <device-name>-vk -o yaml | grep -E "enable-write-class-gnoi|enable-iosxesoftwareupgrade"
kubectl -n <device-namespace> logs deploy/<device-name>-vk --tail=200 | grep -i gnoi

In managed topology, inspect the separate network-management worker using the label-based commands in gather the basics. It must have readWrite access for mutations; the app-hosting worker is not the software-upgrade executor.

If the CR remains untouched, verify the spec.deviceRef.name matches the device worker's CiscoDevice name and that the VK service account can update the CR status and finalizer subresources.

docs.title: Secure gNOI authentication or connection fails
docs.text:
IOS-XE 17.18.x serves password-authenticated gNOI on the secure gNXI listener, port 9339 by default. Start by comparing the device and CiscoDevice settings:

# IOS-XE CLI
show running-config | include ^gnxi
show gnxi state detail
show crypto pki trustpoints

# Kubernetes; this displays references and transport settings, not Secret data
kubectl -n <device-namespace> get ciscodevice <device-name> \
  -o jsonpath='{.spec.username}{"\n"}{.spec.gnoi}{"\n"}{.spec.xe.gnoi}{"\n"}{.spec.tls}{"\n"}'

kubectl -n <device-namespace> logs deploy/<device-name>-vk --tail=200 | grep -iE 'gnoi|gnxi|grpc|x509'

The worker startup log reports trust_source=system, shared, gnoi, or xe-provisioning and auth_mode=iosxe-password-metadata (or none) for explicit TLS without logging certificate or credential contents.

Symptom / gRPC status Most likely cause Check Admission rejects spec.gnoi.tls The transport is not explicitly TLS, file paths were placed in a Kubernetes object, or provisioning is also configured Set spec.gnoi.transportSecurity: tls, use only gnoi.tls.secretRef in Kubernetes, and choose either generic gNOI TLS or spec.xe.gnoi.certificateProvisioning, not both. GNOITLSInvalid event or reconcile error The referenced Secret is missing, ca.crt is empty/invalid, or only one client-certificate key is present Keep the Secret in the CiscoDevice namespace. Supply a parseable ca.crt and either both tls.crt and tls.key or neither. Unauthenticated Missing or rejected metadata Check spec.username, the referenced Secret's exact password key, and gnxi secure-password-auth. CVK sends separate lowercase username and password metadata only over TLS. PermissionDenied Authentication succeeded but AAA denied the RPC Check the IOS-XE AAA method list, user privilege, and authorization policy for the requested operation. x509 trust or hostname error The selected trust source does not validate the certificate or spec.address Check the logged trust source. Update the generic gNOI TLS Secret's ca.crt, or, for provisioning only, supply the exact temporary leaf as bootstrap.crt. Explicit secure/dedicated gNOI has no skip-verification mode. Trust Secret changed but failures persist The enabled per-device worker has not completed its Secret-driven restart Check the per-device Deployment rollout and controller events. Generic TLS Secret rotation affects new connections only and never rotates the device certificate. There is no worker restart in aggregated config-only topology or while gNOI is globally disabled. Startup reports gNOI: resolve configuration The selected trust sources conflict, certificate files are invalid, explicit TLS inherited insecure shared TLS, or CISCO_VK_GNOI_PORT is invalid Correct the named validation error. CVK does not silently downgrade transport, ignore an invalid port override, or fall back to another trust source. Unavailable, connection refused, or deadline exceeded Listener, port, route, firewall, VRF, or expected gNXI restart Check port 9339, show gnxi state detail, pod reachability, and recent provisioning events. FailedPrecondition: Device has not been provisioned Authentication works, but the OS service lacks a provisioned identity Confirm gnxi enable-gnoi and gnxi secure-init, configure spec.xe.gnoi.certificateProvisioning, enable write-class gNOI, and create a ProvisionCertificate action. GNOIOSVerify never installs. ProvisioningUnavailable The worker has no authorized certificate provisioner Confirm spec.xe.gnoi.certificateProvisioning and the write-class gate, and ensure the gated Secret projection contains a valid ca.key; the action is rejected before device access. ProvisioningIntentMismatch The action was created for a different certificate ID or public-material digest than the worker loaded Recompute SHA-256 over the exact tls.crt bytes followed by ca.crt, wait for the Secret-driven worker rollout, then create a new immutable action. No device RPC was sent for the rejected action. Missing ca.key The Secret is in post-provision/read-only form, or the write-class gate is disabled The built-in provisioner/action is available only with the dedicated intermediate CA key and write-class gate, even if OS.Verify might make the action a no-op. Never supply a root CA key. CSR InvalidArgument The profile or signer is invalid Check that tls.crt has C, ST, O, OU, and an IP SAN and chains through the intermediate whose key is in ca.key. Certificate ID conflict / already exists The create-only ID is stale or belongs to another identity Compare GNOICertGet with device trustpoints. Resolve or remove stale state out of band, or choose a new ID; CVK will not overwrite it. Unimplemented That platform does not implement the requested service Use GNOICertGet as the broad pre-provision connectivity probe. GNOIOSVerify is also read-only before provisioning, but only the exact not-provisioned response is expected; success requires State: Provisioned.

Before creating the action, use one of the two starting states documented in the IOS-XE upgrade and downgrade runbook: secure-init for temporary bootstrap, or secure-trustpoint plus secure-server for an already-provisioned identity. Both paths require gnxi enable-gnoi and gnxi secure-password-auth. After a mutation, the action reconnects and succeeds only when the exact installed certificate is the active TLS leaf and OS.Verify works over that same peer; it never retries Install. If OS.Verify already succeeds, the action is a no-op and its requested certificate ID/digest are intent only, not an attestation of the active identity. Confirm the trustpoint and State: Provisioned on the device, then remove ca.key and bootstrap.crt and disable write-class gNOI. See the canonical secure gNOI workflow for configuration, Secret contents, and the shared gNXI/gNMI CA-bundle warning.

docs.title: IOSXEOperationalAction is rejected
docs.text:
Common rejection reasons:

  • ConfirmMismatch — spec.confirm must exactly equal spec.deviceRef.name.
  • InvalidAction — exactly one typed args block must match spec.action.kind.
  • Kubernetes admission rejects updates because spec is immutable after creation. Create a new action CR for a changed request.

For actions that reach Running and then fail, inspect both events and status:

kubectl describe iosxeoperationalaction <name>
kubectl get events --field-selector involvedObject.name=<name>

Running means the controller may already have invoked the device-side RPC. The reconciler will not dispatch the same CR again after a restart. It waits for the bounded RPC-and-persistence window, then records ActionOutcomeUnknown, removes the finalizer so deletion can complete, and retains the shared mutation Lease until its normal expiry. Verify the device's actual state before submitting a replacement action.

docs.title: IOSXESoftwareUpgrade fails during resolution, staging, or transfer
docs.text:
For URL sources, imageSource.sha256 is required. URL userinfo is rejected; query strings and fragments remain visible in the immutable CR even though CVK redacts them from status, events, logs, and errors, so do not put secrets there. For SCP/SFTP, host-key verification is required unless a custom/local deployment explicitly enables both parts of the lab-only escape hatch (the stock Helm chart intentionally does not expose it):

imageSource:
  url: sftp://images.example.net/image.bin?insecureSkipHostKey=true

export CISCO_VK_UPGRADE_ALLOW_INSECURE_SSH=true

image exceeds configured size limit means an HTTP Content-Length, remote file-size report, SCP header, or the streamed bytes exceeded CISCO_VK_UPGRADE_MAX_IMAGE_BYTES. The Helm equivalent is gnoi.softwareUpgrade.maxImageBytes; it defaults to 8 GiB. Do not simply raise the limit: URL resolution stores one full image plus small filesystem and pod overhead in the pod's /tmp emptyDir. The resolver hashes into a private temporary file, atomically promotes that same file to the cache, retains at most one completed managed digest, and removes owned crash residue before the next resolution. Check pod eviction events, node ephemeral-storage pressure, and storage requests/limits.

Transient network, HTTP 408/425/429/5xx, and Kubernetes API read failures remain in Transferring with reason ImageResolveRetry and retry only until installTimeoutSeconds expires. A resolver's shorter per-attempt timeout does not end the upgrade while that overall deadline remains. Credential, endpoint-binding, host-key or TLS verification, malformed source, size, digest, and unsafe-cache errors fail immediately as ImageResolveFailed.

An unsafe image cache entry error means the digest path is a symlink or is not a regular file. CVK will not follow or overwrite it. Treat unexpected cache mutation as a security signal. After confirming no upgrade RPC is in flight, replace the affected worker pod to clear its ephemeral cache.

preinstalled: {} and deprecated localPath require targetVersion to resolve to one exact, activatable install-inventory entry. A matching file on flash is not sufficient. localPathSHA256, when supplied, verifies the legacy path but does not register it.

Use deviceFile.path plus required deviceFile.sha256 when a file already on IOS-XE must be registered. CVK reads it through gNOI File.Get before the IOS-XE RESTCONF install RPC. DeviceFileHashFailed, SoftwareLifecycleUnsupported, AmbiguousTargetVersion, or TargetNotActivatable are fail-closed outcomes; there is no CLI fallback. UncorrelatedDeviceFileInventory means the target was already installed or in progress before this CR recorded its staging request, so CVK cannot prove that the verified file produced that inventory entry. If status reports an unknown staging or activation outcome, inspect the IOS-XE install inventory and operation UUID before creating a new CR. The original CR is not replayed after an ambiguous device mutation. installTimeoutSeconds first bounds gNOI readiness and device-file File.Get. The native-registration claim then starts a fresh window shared by registration and inventory convergence; retries inside either window receive only its remaining time.

MutationLeaseBlocked means another CVK-managed write action, upgrade, or uncertain prior outcome owns the device's shared disruptive-mutation Lease. Inspect that object's status and the Lease holder identity. Do not delete the Lease merely to bypass an unknown device result; wait for the safety TTL or establish device state before taking an explicitly controlled recovery action.

After gNOI OS.Install is dispatched, a transport interruption moves the CR to TransferInterrupted. CVK retains the durable attempt marker and observes without replay until installTimeoutSeconds expires, even when native inventory reports the target absent. The CR then fails with InstallOutcomeUnknown; inspect the device before creating a new upgrade CR.

With rollbackOnFailure: true, a verify mismatch enters RollingBack and attempts to re-activate the previously observed running version only when the lifecycle backend proves it remains activatable. If no previous version was captured, the CR fails with RollbackVersionMissing. Rollback receives a new rebootTimeoutSeconds timer when that phase begins, including any pre-dispatch reachability wait; its activation RPC is capped by the remaining time. The primary activation sequence follows the same remaining-time cap. After a durable mutation claim, ActivationControlTimeout or RollbackDidNotConverge retains the shared Lease until its safety TTL expires.

strategy: ISSU fails preflight with ISSUVerificationUnsupported. CVK does not claim a non-disruptive upgrade until the platform backend can verify that IOS-XE selected the ISSU path; NoReboot is not that verification.

docs.title: OTEL traces not appearing
docs.text:
Check it's enabled:

kubectl get ciscodevice <name> -o yaml | yq .spec.otel

Verify VK pod startup:

kubectl logs deploy/<device-name>-vk | grep -i otel

You should see one of:

  • OTEL topology exporter started — good, emitting
  • Failed to initialise OTEL topology exporter — endpoint unreachable or config invalid
  • driver does not implement TopologyProvider — wrong driver (FAKE doesn't, XE does)

Common misconfigurations:

  • endpoint has scheme prefix (wrong): https://otel:4317. Use host:port only.
  • insecure: false against a plaintext gRPC collector — use insecure: true for typical in-cluster OTLP collectors without TLS.
  • intervalSecs set below 10 — the minimum is enforced to 10 s; values below will silently use 60 s.

No traces after 60 s: check the collector logs — it will receive spans in batches. Splunk Observability Cloud can sometimes take a minute to surface the first trace.

docs.title: Symptom
docs.text:
kubectl describe pod <name> shows the container in a waiting state:

State:          Waiting
  Reason:       PullingImage
  Message:      Copying image to device flash; this may take several minutes

docs.title: What is happening
docs.text:
The VK attempted a device-native HTTP pull that timed out (default 3 minutes), and is now running the copy fallback: it downloads the image tar from the HTTP URL and copies it to device flash via RESTCONF, then reinstalls from that local path. The copy RPC is synchronous and can take several minutes depending on image size and network speed.

You can monitor progress via pod events:

kubectl describe pod <name>
# Look for the Events section at the bottom:
#
#   Normal  Pulling          <time>   cisco-virtual-kubelet  Pulling image https://...
#   Warning ImagePullFallback <time>  cisco-virtual-kubelet  Device-native pull timed out...
#   Normal  Copying          <time>   cisco-virtual-kubelet  Copying image ... to flash:/...
#   Normal  Pulled           <time>   cisco-virtual-kubelet  Image successfully copied to ...
#   Normal  Started          <time>   cisco-virtual-kubelet  App ... is running

docs.title: Wait times
docs.text:
• A 500 MB image over a 100 Mb/s management link takes roughly 40 seconds for the copy alone, plus 30 seconds for app activation. Allow 3–5 minutes total.
  • If the pod does not transition to Running after 10 minutes, check VK logs for errors:
kubectl -n <device-namespace> logs deploy/<device-name>-vk | grep -E "copy|fallback|error|Error"

docs.title: Avoiding the copy fallback
docs.text:
To use the copy path intentionally and skip the device-native pull attempt entirely, set imagePullPolicy: Never and pre-copy the tar to flash yourself. Then reference the flash path directly in the pod spec:

image: flash:/virtual-kubelet/my-app.tar
imagePullPolicy: Never

docs.title: imagePullPolicy: IfNotPresent still re-downloads the image every time
Symptom
docs.text: You set imagePullPolicy: IfNotPresent expecting the image to be reused from a local cache, but each pod creation issues a fresh download. dir flash: shows no cached tar.

docs.title: Why
docs.text:
IOS-XE App Hosting does not leave a copy of the image on flash when using the device-native install path (app-hosting install appid ... package <url>). The device fetches and loads the image directly into the container runtime without writing it to flash. Since no flash copy is ever created, there is nothing for IfNotPresent to reuse — it behaves identically to Always on the device-native pull path.

The IfNotPresent flash-cache optimization only activates when the VK's copy fallback path has run at least once (i.e., the device-native pull timed out and the VK copied the tar to flash itself). After that first copy, subsequent deploys with IfNotPresent will reuse the cached tar.

docs.title: Workaround
docs.text:
To reliably benefit from local caching, force the copy path by one of the following:

  • Pre-copy the image to flash manually on the device, then use imagePullPolicy: Never with a flash path (flash:/virtual-kubelet/my-app.tar).
  • Accept that on platforms where the device-native pull succeeds quickly, re-downloading from the registry on each deploy is the expected behaviour.

See also Image Distribution for serving registry images over HTTP.

docs.title: Symptom
docs.text:
Pod immediately goes to Failed with:

status:
  phase: Failed
  message: "app ...: imagePullPolicy is Never but image is an HTTP URL ..."

docs.title: Why
docs.text: imagePullPolicy: Never means the image must already exist on device flash and no download of any kind will be attempted. Using an HTTP or HTTPS URL with this policy is invalid.

docs.title: Fix
docs.text:
Either:

  1. Change the image reference to a flash path: flash:/virtual-kubelet/my-app.tar
  2. Or change the imagePullPolicy to IfNotPresent or Always to allow the VK to download it.

docs.title: Pod stuck Failed forever
docs.text:
Usually one of:

  • reason: NotFound — VK pod was restarted and lost state. The pod recovery loop handles this automatically.
  • reason: ProviderFailed — transient device issue. Recovery loop handles this.
  • reason: PackagePolicyInvalid — see above.

The pod recovery loop resets matching Failed pods to Pending with exponential backoff (15 s → 5 min). You should see this in VK logs:

Recovered <n> stale failed pods

If the loop isn't running, check the VK pod is healthy (not crash-looping). The recovery goroutine starts with the rest of the VK and stops when the VK exits.

docs.title: Virtual node lingers after CiscoDevice deletion
docs.text:
Normally the controller deletes the virtual Node as part of finalizer cleanup. If you see a lingering node:

kubectl get node <device-name>
# Status: NotReady

This usually means the finalizer was skipped (force-delete of the CR, or the controller was down when deletion happened). Clean up by hand:

kubectl delete node <device-name>

Check no orphaned Deployment / ConfigMap remains:

kubectl -n <ns> get deploy,cm | grep <device-name>

Avoid kubectl delete ciscodevice --force --grace-period=0 — it skips the finalizer and will cause this.

docs.title: A Secret update did not roll the VK pod
docs.text:
The controller normally watches referenced credential Secrets and copies their resourceVersion into the Deployment pod template, which triggers an automatic rollout. Compare the source and observed versions and check the manager:

kubectl -n <ns> get secret <secret-name> \
  -o jsonpath='{.metadata.resourceVersion}{"\n"}'
kubectl -n <ns> get deploy/<device-name>-vk \
  -o jsonpath='{.spec.template.metadata.annotations.cisco\.vk/credential-resource-version}{"\n"}'
kubectl -n cvk-system get deploy,pods
kubectl -n cvk-system logs deploy/cvk-cisco-virtual-kubelet-controller --tail=200

Confirm the CiscoDevice references that same-namespace Secret. After fixing the manager or reference, the watch-driven reconcile should roll the pod. For an immediate troubleshooting fallback, force one manually:

kubectl -n <ns> rollout restart deploy/<device-name>-vk

docs.title: Where to look next
docs.text:
• Architecture — internal state machines and data flow
  • Configuration — every field and its defaults
  • Observability — metrics and OTEL details
  • GitHub issues — if your problem isn't listed here, file an issue with:
  • CiscoDevice spec (redact credentials)
  • kubectl describe ciscodevice output
  • VK pod logs (--tail=200)
  • show app-hosting detail appid <id> from the device

docs.title: YANG Version Support for IOS-XE Writers
Overview
docs.text:
IOS-XE YANG models change across firmware versions. The NAC (Network as Code) writers are authored against a baseline version (currently 17.18.2 on C9300-24P). Earlier versions (17.15, 17.16) diverge in several ways:

  • Module prefixes required on augmented JSON body keys
  • Different YANG list-key names (e.g. ordering-seq vs seq)
  • Empty-leaf encoding ([null] instead of boolean true)
  • Different container shapes (flat ↔ nested, keyed list ↔ container)
  • Different RESTCONF paths and envelope keys

docs.title: Per-family schema validation
docs.text:
CVK uses goyang-extracted, per-family Go schema packages as CI-time validators. For each config family the generator navigates the resolved native YANG entry tree to the terminal container or list declared in yang_paths, serialises that sub-tree to a gzip-JSON blob, and embeds it as a ySchema byte literal in schema.go. This approach avoids ygot code generation entirely — no 125 MB generated files, no 32 GB memory peaks.

Runtime is unchanged. The override table, map-shaped writers, and engine are not modified by this system. The generated packages are never imported at runtime — they register a cfgvalidation.FamilySchemaValidator from their init() function, and the fixture harness calls Lookup(family, releaseTag) to validate every op body against the schema during go test.

BUILD / CI TIME
  families.yaml (yang_paths per family)
      │
      ▼
  computeModuleClosure() — goyang BFS over import+include graph
      │  produces minimal module set per family
      ▼
  extractFamilySchemaEntries() — ms.Process() resolves augments;
      │  navigates nativeEntry.Dir to terminal container/list
      ▼
  buildFamilyYSchema() — gzip-JSON blob of the terminal entry sub-tree
      │
      ▼
  internal/drivers/iosxe/configdriver/generated/<release>/<family>/
    schema.go    (goyang-based gzip blob, UnzipSchema function)
    register.go  (calls cfgvalidation.Register from init())

CI VALIDATOR (fixture_test.go)
  writer.Diff() → expected_ops.json op bodies
      │
      ▼
  validateOpsAgainstGeneratedSchema()
      │
      ├── validator registered  → validateJSONEntry() — structural check
      └── no validator          → silently skipped (incremental rollout)

Generated packages live under internal/drivers/iosxe/configdriver/generated/. They are committed to the repo so runtime builds do not need the YANG source bundle. CI runs the pinned generator and verifies that the committed packages have no tracked or untracked drift. The make ygot-validate-gen RELEASE=<tag> target regenerates one release from a clean output directory.

Schema coverage limitations. Each family's schema is extracted from a module closure computed by tracing import/include graphs outward from the modules named in yang_paths. Modules that augment the native tree (e.g. Cisco-IOS-XE-aaa) are not found by this traversal unless they appear as a Module: prefix in the family's yang_paths. When augmenting modules are absent the terminal entry's Dir is empty and the validator skips that container rather than producing false positives.

Skip policy. A family is skipped (emits a compilable stub schema.go) when:

  • its yang_paths resolve to no module prefixes in the YANG directory,
  • the extracted schema blob exceeds 512 KB (e.g. system with /native as its target — the entire native tree), or
  • the path is not present in the YANG model for that release.

Those are domain limitations, not general error handling. Parser, schema-builder, filesystem, registration, and validator-index errors fail generation immediately. The exact expected release/family/reason-code set is stored in schema/yang-skip-baseline.yaml; an added skip, resolved skip, or reason change fails generation until the baseline and regenerated artifacts are intentionally updated together. generated/SKIPLIST.md is the human summary. There are currently 35 usable validators and 19 reviewed skip stubs per supported release.

Validation strictness mode. By default the validator is lenient: unknown fields and structural type mismatches are silently skipped so fixtures that reference deprecated YANG paths or fields from augmenting modules outside the closure do not fail CI. Set CVK_SCHEMA_VALIDATION=strict to enable strict mode, which reports these discrepancies as hard errors:

# Surface all YANG schema discrepancies in fixture data:
CVK_SCHEMA_VALIDATION=strict \
  go test ./internal/drivers/iosxe/configdriver/writers/... -run TestFixtures

Strict-mode failures indicate one of: - a fixture uses a field name not present in the YANG schema for that release (e.g. a deprecated or augmented field — fix by updating the fixture), - the schema closure is incomplete and the augmenting module needs to be added to the family's yang_paths (e.g. a Module:field prefix is missing).

The default lenient mode keeps CI green while these root causes are addressed incrementally. See generated/SKIPLIST.md for the current skip list.

docs.title: Intent, Translation, Validation Boundary
docs.text:
CVK keeps the public IOSXEConfig.spec.source payload in the canonical NetAsCode shape. That shape is intentionally release-stable: operators should not have to change day-0 YAML just because IOS-XE moved a leaf or renamed an augmented container between 17.18 and 26.01.

The release-specific boundary is therefore:

NetAsCode intent
  -> family writer
  -> version override / body transform
  -> IOS-XE YANG JSON op
  -> validation boundary
  -> RESTCONF / NETCONF / gNMI transport

internal/drivers/iosxe/configdriver/validation owns the validation boundary. It runs after writers emit transport.Op values and before the engine calls Apply. The default StructuralValidator checks common op invariants (path scope, JSON envelope shape, body presence) and hosts narrow release profiles for known divergences. IOS-XE 26.01 currently validates that ip_domain.name has been translated to name-container.name-no-vrf before mutation.

This is the seam where generated ygot/ytypes validators belong once per-release config model packages are available. ygot should validate the device-facing YANG payload, not replace the public NetAsCode intent model.

Validation is deployment-policy controlled:

Mode Effect CONFIG_YANG_VALIDATION=disabled default; no validation gate CONFIG_YANG_VALIDATION=warn log validation failures and continue CONFIG_YANG_VALIDATION=strict fail the family before mutation

The Helm value is config.yangValidationMode. The controller propagates it to per-device VK pods so aggregator mode and per-pod mode use the same policy.

docs.title: Stable NetAsCode Import Contract
docs.text:
For customer migrations from Terraform-based NetAsCode, CVK imports the resolved NetAsCode IOS-XE model and records provenance in IOSXEConfig.spec.modelSource. This keeps the public intent model stable while the writer layer handles IOS-XE release differences.

spec:
  modelSource:
    format: netascode-iosxe
    resolved: true
    exporter: terraform-iosxe-nac-iosxe write_model_file

resolved: false is rejected by the resolver. If a future NetAsCode release adds fields, CVK should first accept the canonical data model shape, then either translate the field for the target YANG release or report it as an unsupported family/field through migration tooling and validation. The CRD should not fork by IOS-XE release.

docs.title: Override Table (yang_version_override_table.go)
docs.text:
The declarative override table is the central registry of version- conditional YANG behaviour. Each entry targets a (family, version_range) and describes mutations to apply to the YANG wire representation.

┌──────────────────────────────────────┐
│  Override Table Entry                │
│                                      │
│  Family:              "route_map"    │
│  MinVersion:          [17, 0]        │
│  MaxVersion:          [17, 18]       │
│  ElementMap:          { old → new }  │
│  NestedYANGInnerOverride: "..."      │
│  YANGPathOverride:    "..."          │
│  EnvelopeKeyOverride: "..."          │
│  EmptyLeaves:         ["prefer"]     │
│  BodyTransform:       func(...)      │
└──────────────────────────────────────┘

The table is resolved once at startup via ResolveForVersion(major, minor). Writers query the resolved state at Diff/Apply time:

Query Function Purpose IsLegacyVersion(fam) Is the device on a pre-baseline version? ResolvedYANGPath(fam, default) Version-correct RESTCONF path ResolvedEnvelopeKey(fam, default) Version-correct JSON envelope ResolvedNestedYANGInner(fam, default) Version-correct inner list name ApplyOverrideToBody(body, override) Full transform chain

docs.title: Custom Version-Branched Writers
docs.text:
Three families have structural YANG differences too deep for the override table alone:

Family Mechanism bgp Keyed list (17.16) vs container (17.18+) prefix_list Flat compound-keyed (17.16) vs nested (17.18+) ip_community_list Deprecated groupings (17.16) vs community-list-entry (17.18+)

These writers use IsLegacyVersion() to select their code path, and the override table provides path/envelope selection. Transform logic is per-writer.

docs.title: YAML 1.1 Boolean Key Fix
docs.text: sigs.k8s.io/yaml (YAML 1.1) interprets bare no as boolean false, which becomes map key "false" in map[string]any. This is fixed globally by intent.FixYAML11BoolKeys(), which runs once on the fully-merged configuration tree at the end of Resolver.Resolve().

docs.title: Adding Support for a New IOS-XE Version
1. Identify divergences
docs.text:
Compare the YANG schemas between the new version and the baseline:

# Download YANG models from the device
curl -k https://<device>/restconf/.well-known/host-meta

# Or use Cisco's published YANG repo:
# https://github.com/YangModels/yang/tree/main/vendor/cisco/xe

Use pyang --tree-diff or yanglint to diff specific modules:

pyang -f tree --tree-path /native/ip/prefix-list \
  Cisco-IOS-XE-native-17.16.yang \
  Cisco-IOS-XE-native-17.18.yang

For RESTCONF, probe the device directly:

# GET the schema for a specific path
curl -k -u admin:pass \
  'https://<device>/restconf/data/Cisco-IOS-XE-native:native/ip/prefix-list' \
  -H 'Accept: application/yang-data+json'

docs.title: 2. Classify the divergence
docs.text: Type Fix Mechanism Module prefix needed on element key ElementMap in override table Different YANG path or envelope YANGPathOverride / EnvelopeKeyOverride Boolean → empty leaf encoding EmptyLeaves in override table Simple container shape change BodyTransform function Key field rename KeyFieldOverride or ElementMap Deep structural difference Custom writer with IsLegacyVersion()

docs.title: 3. Add the table entry
docs.text:
Add an entry to yang_version_override_table.go:

{
    Family:     "new_family",
    MinVersion: [2]int{17, 0},
    MaxVersion: [2]int{17, 20},  // exclusive upper bound
    ElementMap: map[string]string{
        "baseline-name": "Cisco-IOS-XE-module:version-name",
    },
},

docs.title: 4. Write tests
docs.text:
• Add transform tests to version_transforms_test.go
  • Add override resolution tests to yang_version_overrides_test.go
  • Add structural validation coverage for any release-specific YANG payload shape in internal/drivers/iosxe/configdriver/validation
  • Run integration tests on a device of that version

docs.title: 5. Verify
docs.text:
# Unit tests
go test ./internal/drivers/iosxe/configdriver/writers/ -v
go test ./internal/drivers/iosxe/configdriver/validation -v

# Full build
go build ./...

# Integration tests (on lab device)
pytest tests/test_monolithic_router.py -v

docs.title: Reference: CiscoDevNet/terraform-provider-iosxe
docs.text: The Terraform provider for IOS-XE is an excellent reference for correct YANG paths and data structures. It was instrumental in discovering the 17.16 prefix-lists (plural) path with the flat compound-keyed prefixes[name, no] list.

docs.title: Reference: Known YAML 1.1 Boolean Keys
docs.text:
YAML 1.1 treats these bare tokens as booleans when used as map keys:

Token JSON key Canonical name no "false" "no" yes "true" (not used in IOS-XE schema) on "true" (not used in IOS-XE schema) off "false" (not used in IOS-XE schema)

The yaml11BoolKeyMap in intent/yaml11_fix.go maps only keys that actually appear in the IOS-XE netascode schema. Add entries there if future schema keys collide with YAML 1.1 booleans.

docs.title: Nexus Dashboard controller adapter
docs.text:
Alpha · introduced in v2026.11.1. Use matching CRDs, chart and image; October v2026.10.0 does not contain this adapter. Check the release records for publication and artifact availability.

The nexus-dashboard adapter connects a NetworkController to Cisco Nexus Dashboard (ND) 4.x through the /api/v1 APIs (Infra login, Manage). It does not use the NDFC legacy /appcenter/... APIs.

Scope: the adapter connects and authenticates, reports health and the ND version, reads the switch inventory, and can optionally adopt the switches as standalone CiscoDevice objects (see Device adoption). It does not reconcile Network as Code intent: the stripe is nd, declared but not reconciled.

docs.title: What it checks
docs.text:
Every spec.connection.healthCheckInterval (default 1m) the worker:

  1. Logs in with POST /api/v1/infra/login using the mounted credentials.
  2. Calls GET /api/v1/manage/fabrics with the AuthCookie token.
  3. After a successful probe, reads GET /api/v1/infra/about and publishes the ND product version (for example 4.3.1) as status.controllerVersion. This is informational: a failure neither changes health nor clears the last known version. The pre-login banner in that response is never read.
  4. Writes Authenticated, APICompatible, Ready, the health capability, phase, and the attempt/success timestamps to status.
Outcome Authenticated APICompatible Phase Login and Manage API succeed True True Ready Bad credentials (401/403 on login) False False Error Missing or empty credential files False False Error Login works, Manage API 404 True False Degraded Login works, Manage API 403 True False Degraded Unreachable, TLS failure, 5xx, 429 False False Degraded

Messages are redacted and limited to 512 characters. Tokens and passwords never reach status, events, or logs. The token is cached and rebuilt on projected credential/CA rotation, after MaxSessionLifetime, and once after a 401 on a read request. Only GET requests are retried.

docs.title: Inventory
docs.text:
Every 5 minutes (jittered by 10%) the worker lists fabrics with GET /api/v1/manage/fabrics, then the switches of each fabric with GET /api/v1/manage/fabrics/{fabricName}/switches, following meta.counts.remaining. Each switch becomes an in-memory InventoryItem (serial from switchId, hostname, management address from fabricManagementIp, model, software version, fabric, and reachability from additionalData.discoveryStatus == ok).

  • A switch is adoptable only if its model looks like NX-OS (N9K-...), and it has a serial and a management address. Others are skipped with a reason.
  • The inventory capability in status.capabilities reports counts only, for example 4 switches in 1 fabrics; 2 adoptable NX-OS, 1 unreachable, 1 skipped. Adoptable means NX-OS and reachable (ND discoveryStatus is ok), the same rule device adoption applies; unreachable counts NX-OS switches ND cannot currently reach. This is reported even when adoption is off. Serials, hostnames, and addresses are never written to status or logs.
  • If any fabric fails to list, the whole refresh fails and the last complete snapshot is kept; the capability shows Supported=false with a redacted reason. The same applies to a response that cannot be trusted to be complete: an empty page while ND still reports items remaining, or a response with no fabrics/switches list (a missing list is accepted only as the first page of a collection ND itself reports as empty). A partial snapshot is never used, so it can never cause a device to be marked missing or pruned.
  • There is no fabric or role filter. role comes from ND's switchRole.
  • Inventory only becomes CiscoDevice objects when device adoption is enabled (next section).

docs.title: Device adoption
docs.text:
Off by default. With spec.deviceAdoption.enabled: true, every reachable NX-OS switch from a complete inventory refresh becomes a standalone CiscoDevice (driver NXOS) in the NetworkController's namespace.

Adoption is never automatic. A NetworkController without deviceAdoption, or with enabled: false, only reads and reports ND inventory and never creates, updates or deletes a CiscoDevice. No Helm value turns it on. Setting enabled back to false stops all further writes: devices that were already adopted stay in place, unchanged, and are not pruned. The device-adoption capability appears in status only while adoption is enabled and has run: the worker rebuilds the whole status.capabilities list on every publish, so status never reports adoption as active when it is not.

spec:
  deviceAdoption:
    enabled: true
    defaults:                       # required when enabled
      username: admin
      credentialSecretRef: {name: switch-creds}   # key "password"
      tls: {enabled: true, insecureSkipVerify: true}
    scopeOverrides:                 # per ND fabric; omitted fields inherit
      - scope: dc2-fabric
        credentialSecretRef: {name: dc2-switch-creds}

docs.title: Labels for grouping devices
docs.text:
defaults.labels and scopeOverrides[].labels add your own labels to every adopted device, for example to group switches into upgrade waves:

spec:
  deviceAdoption:
    defaults:
      labels: {upgrade-wave: "1", owner: netops}
    scopeOverrides:
      - scope: dc2-fabric
        labels: {upgrade-wave: "2"}      # merged per key over the defaults

They are written to metadata.labels (for kubectl get ciscodevices -l upgrade-wave=2) and to spec.labels (projected onto the Node, for nodeSelector). Labels users add themselves are never touched. A label you remove from the NetworkController is removed from the devices again, because the adapter records the keys it applied in the annotation cisco.vk/nd-managed-labels. The nd.cisco.vk/, cisco.vk/, topology.cisco.vk/ and kubernetes.io/k8s.io namespaces are reserved, and at most 16 labels are allowed per block. CVK does not act on these labels itself; something else, such as a Job with a nodeSelector, has to.

docs.title: Removing devices
docs.text:
spec:
  deviceAdoption:
    removal:
      policy: Prune          # Retain (default) | Prune
      gracePeriod: 24h       # 10m - 720h, default 24h
      maxPrunePercent: 25    # default 25

With Prune, an adopted CiscoDevice is deleted once it has been missing for the grace period (measured from the annotation, so it survives worker restarts). Deleting the CiscoDevice makes the CiscoDevice controller remove the worker and the Node. Guards:

  • only devices with this controller's UID label are ever deleted;
  • an empty inventory marks and deletes nothing;
  • if more than maxPrunePercent of the adopted devices are due at once, nothing is deleted and they are reported as prune-guarded (one device is always allowed, so a small fleet can still shrink);
  • delete uses a UID precondition.

The worker role carries the delete verb for this. RBAC cannot depend on the policy, so every ND worker holds it, even with Retain.

ND does not expose device passwords, so the operator supplies them. The adapter writes only the Secret name and never reads the Secret; it has no Secrets permission. Create the Secret in the same namespace, with a password key, like any other CiscoDevice credential.

What gets created, per switch:

  • name nd-<serial> (lowercased, unsafe characters replaced; long serials get a hash suffix), spec.physicalIdentity = serial, spec.address = ND's fabric management IP;
  • spec.nodeName = the ND hostname, set only at creation and only when the hostname is already a valid Node name, unique in ND, and not used by another CiscoDevice. Otherwise it is left empty and the name defaults to metadata.name. It is immutable, so later hostname changes in ND do not rename the Node;
  • labels nd.cisco.vk/fabric, nd.cisco.vk/role, nd.cisco.vk/model on both the CiscoDevice and its Node;
  • ownership label cisco.vk/network-controller-uid. There is deliberately no ownerReference, so deleting the NetworkController does not garbage-collect devices and Nodes.

Safety rules:

  • The adapter only touches CiscoDevices that carry its controller's UID label. A device with the same name that it did not create is counted as a name conflict and left alone.
  • Updates are merge patches of the fields the adapter owns (address, username, secret, TLS, labels). Labels, ports, taints and other fields that users add are kept.
  • Adoption runs only after a complete successful refresh. A failed or empty refresh changes nothing.
  • Before every device write (create, update, annotate, delete) the worker re-reads its NetworkController from the API server and writes nothing unless it is still the active binding: same UID and generation, not paused or being deleted, and spec.deviceAdoption.enabled still true. A worker that was superseded during a rollout, or that cannot confirm this, stops without writing, so it cannot keep creating, updating or pruning devices after adoption was disabled or the controller paused.
  • A device whose switch is missing from a complete refresh gets the annotation cisco.vk/nd-missing-since (first-seen time, RFC 3339). It is removed again if the switch returns. An unreachable or non-NX-OS switch is still in ND and is not "missing". By default (policy Retain) nothing is ever deleted.
  • Unreachable switches (discoveryStatus not ok), non-NX-OS switches, and switches with a serial that is not a valid physicalIdentity are not adopted.
  • The device-adoption capability reports counts only, for example 2 created, 0 updated, 1 unchanged; 0 unreachable, 0 invalid, 0 name conflicts, 0 failed; 0 missing, 0 pruned, 0 prune-guarded.

The ND worker is bound to cisco-virtual-kubelet-nd-worker: the base worker role plus get/list/watch/create/update/patch on ciscodevices (delete but no deletecollection, no Secrets, no ciscodevices/status). The role is static, so an ND worker holds it even when adoption is disabled.

docs.title: Credential Secret
docs.text:
The Secret is mounted read-only; the worker reads one file per key:

Key Required Notes username yes ND local or remote-auth user. A read-only role is enough. password yes domain no ND login domain. Defaults to local. 
kubectl create secret generic nd-credentials \
  --from-literal=username=cvk-reader \
  --from-literal=password='...' \
  --from-literal=domain=local

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
apiVersion: cisco.vk/v1alpha1
kind: NetworkController
metadata:
  name: nd-lab
spec:
  type: nexus-dashboard
  endpoint: https://nd.example.com
  credentialSecretRef:
    name: nd-credentials
  tls:
    caConfigMapRef:
      name: nd-ca
      key: ca.crt

TLS verification is on by default. Use tls.caConfigMapRef for a private CA. tls.insecureSkipVerify: true is for controlled labs only and cannot be combined with a CA reference.

Rate limiting defaults to 5 requests per second with a burst of 10, and spec.connection.rateLimit overrides it.

docs.title: Verifying
docs.text:
kubectl get networkcontroller nd-lab
kubectl get networkcontroller nd-lab -o jsonpath='{range .status.conditions[*]}{.type}={.status} {.reason}{"\n"}{end}'

docs.title: API notes
docs.text:
• Login body: {"domain","userName","userPasswd"}; the response carries token (also jwttoken). Requests send Cookie: AuthCookie=<token>.
  • GET /api/v1/infra/about returns productVersion (4.3.1), buildVersion (4.3.1.175) and productName; it was checked on a live ND 4.3.1. The NDFC path /appcenter/cisco/ndfc/api/v1/fm/about/version also answers there but is the legacy API and is not used.
  • Documented example tokens expire about 20 minutes after issue; the adapter refreshes on its own schedule and on 401.
  • The Manage API is GA from ND 4.2.1; Early Access releases may change schemas.
  • The switch schema was checked against a live ND 4.x capture; testdata/switches_page.json is that response with identifiers replaced. The max and offset paging parameters are accepted and offset is honored (an offset past the end returns an empty list). Multi-page inventory was qualified on 2026-10-26 against the lab ND 4.3.1 with a temporary local build using a page size of 1 (not shipped): two switches in one fabric returned offset=0 (1 item, remaining=1, total=2) then offset=1 (1 item, remaining=0, total=2), and the inventory held both switches. Still not observed: more than 100 switches (the shipped page size), multiple fabrics, and ND's total semantics across them, which is why the adapter does not cross-check collected items against total. Prune is opt-in; qualify against a multi-fabric ND before using it in production.

docs.title: SD-WAN implementation and live-test backlog
docs.text:
This is a progress inventory, not a claim of completed deployment parity. The pinned NetAsCode v1.5.0 module contains 226 resource declarations. Current status:

Status Declarations Fixture-qualified against live Manager 218 Implemented with local fixtures; live tests outstanding 7 Implementation still pending 0 Compatibility-blocked (TrustSec) 1

Configuration-group and policy-group device association/deployment now compile from site routers, including scalar/list group variables, topology labels and deploy flags. Their Manager associate/variables/deploy/readback/update workflow passes a local HTTP fixture. Both group association types passed live create/read/disassociate/delete on BR-2-WAN after confirming it had no existing group assignment. Variable upload and deployment remain local-API-tested; live device push still needs a configuration fixture preserving its running system and transport settings. Device-template attachment now compiles from site routers with device_template and device_variables; its Manager config-input/attach/readback/update workflow and Adaptive QoS variable-name lookup pass local HTTP fixtures. Live attachment remains untested; the selected BR-2-WAN has no classic template, but the current fixture carries placeholder system identity and cannot safely be pushed as-is. Topology-group activate: true now compiles as a single activation ordered after its group and passes a local API/task lifecycle test; a live attempt with an isolated site and mesh policy reached the asynchronous task, which failed because the vSmart control component has neither an attached device template nor a control-component setting. Centralized policy activation now compiles from activated_policy, orders after its declared feature policy, and passes a local API/task lifecycle test. A live attempt was rejected with POLICY0006: vSmart 10.255.255.2 is not in vManage mode. Both activation fixtures were removed, and a later Manager inventory showed zero centralized policies and zero topology groups. An unattached classic Cisco BGP template with AS number, router ID and an IPv4 network passed native lifecycle; nested neighbor and route-policy compilation passed local checks. Provider-missing optional-variable fields and the module compare-router-ID variable typo remain explicitly recorded. An unattached classic secure internet gateway template with an other GRE tunnel passed native lifecycle. Provider/tunnel selector derivation and HA-pair compilation have local checks; Umbrella, Zscaler and IPsec variants remain outside the live fixture. An unattached classic cEdge AAA template with local authentication order passed native lifecycle; rule indexing and nested RADIUS-client VPN compilation passed local checks. Other AAA branches remain outside the live fixture. An unattached classic Cisco Ethernet interface template with interface name, IPv4 address and shutdown passed native lifecycle. Its complete generated attribute model remains much broader than the live fixture. Classic Cisco VPN fixtures with ID/name/OMP distance and IPv4/IPv6 DNS servers plus flattened host entries pass native lifecycle and Kubernetes reconciliation. OMP OSPF and global route import/export external subtypes now pass native lifecycle; other route branches remain outside these fixtures. Unattached classic device templates now pass native lifecycle and Kubernetes reconciliation with system/banner references, a nested service VPN containing BGP and Ethernet templates, and localized/security policy bindings. Transport, management and service VPN nesting now passes live lifecycle with Ethernet children, system logging/NTP children and service Ethernet DHCP. Switchport and cellular controller/profile references also pass live lifecycle. Other VPN child families remain outside the live fixtures. The security container-profile reference is live-qualified. NetAsCode site/router tags now compile and preserve existing overlapping tags in a local association test. Tag create, BR-2-WAN association, readback, removal, and cleanup passed live; its prior empty tag state was restored. The classic Cisco system template now has an unattached fixture covering hostname, system IP and site-ID variables, and passed native lifecycle plus Kubernetes reconciliation. Provider-missing endpoint tracker fields and the schema-missing EPFR field remain explicitly rejected. The cloud-provider settings model and local API lifecycle are implemented, but live qualification is outstanding because the lab already contains that global singleton with potentially real credentials. The latest live-qualified increment covers Global network-hierarchy cflowd and security-logging collector settings with native create/read/update/delete and Kubernetes reconciliation. The lab had no pre-existing singleton settings, and both were removed after qualification. The preceding increment qualifies a classic centralized custom-control definition with OMP-tag route match and default reject action. Site-targeted binding and other actions remain outside the fixture. The preceding increment qualifies a classic centralized application-aware routing definition with a source-prefix match and log action. Other SLA-class, match and action variants remain outside the fixture. The preceding increment qualifies a classic centralized traffic-data definition with a source-prefix rule and default drop action. Other match/action variants remain outside the fixture. The preceding increment qualifies a classic zone-based firewall definition with a source-prefix pass rule and resolved self-to-zone pair, plus its security-policy reference. The preceding increment qualifies an unattached classic security-policy assembly with a resolved intrusion-prevention definition through native lifecycle and Kubernetes reconciliation. Manager returns an empty security-policy POST body, so CVK finds the created ID in the list response. The preceding increment qualifies a classic intrusion-prevention definition with detection mode, a balanced signature set, warning logging and target VPN through native lifecycle and Kubernetes reconciliation. The preceding increment qualifies a classic centralized hub-and-spoke definition with separate hub and spoke site lists and includes it in the unattached centralized feature-policy assembly. The preceding increment qualifies an unattached centralized feature-policy assembly with resolved mesh and VPN-membership definitions through native lifecycle and Kubernetes reconciliation. Activation, target routers and other definition families remain outside the fixture. The preceding increment qualifies a classic centralized cflowd definition with a collector. Manager rejects the provider-enumerated exportSpread: disable, so that optional variant remains unqualified. The preceding increment qualifies classic centralized VPN-membership and mesh-topology definitions with resolved site and VPN policy lists through native lifecycle and Kubernetes reconciliation. Other centralized definition families and activation remain outside the fixture. The preceding increment qualifies the localized feature-policy assembly with resolved QoS-map and rewrite-rule definitions through native lifecycle and Kubernetes reconciliation. Other definition families and settings remain outside the fixture. The preceding increment qualifies localized QoS map and rewrite-rule definitions with a resolved classic class-map policy object through native lifecycle and Kubernetes reconciliation. Other scheduler and rewrite variants remain outside the fixture. The preceding increment qualifies a localized route policy definition with OMP-tag match and metric action through native lifecycle and Kubernetes reconciliation. Other route-policy match and action fields remain outside the fixture. The preceding increment qualifies classic localized IPv4 and IPv6 device ACL definitions with a source prefix and supported destination port. Manager requires port 22 or 161 in each device ACL rule and normalizes the IPv6 type casing. The preceding increment qualifies classic localized IPv4 and IPv6 ACL definitions with a direct source-prefix match through native lifecycle and Kubernetes reconciliation. Other match fields, actions and policy assembly remain outside the fixtures. The preceding increment qualifies the embedded-security policy assembly with a resolved NGFW parcel and a self-to-untrusted zone pair. Advanced-inspection references, additional zone types and device deployment remain outside the fixture. The preceding increment qualifies an embedded-security NGFW policy with a source-prefix pass rule. Other match criteria, actions and inspection profiles remain outside the fixture. The preceding increment qualifies an application-priority traffic policy with VPN targeting and a basic sequence. Match entries and actions remain outside the fixture. The preceding increment qualifies an application-priority QoS parcel with interface targeting and no schedulers. Class-map references and scheduler attributes remain outside the fixture. The preceding increment qualifies an unattached policy group referencing application-priority and SSE profiles through native lifecycle and Kubernetes reconciliation. Device association and policy activation are not covered. The preceding increment qualifies a topology group referencing a CVK-created topology profile through native lifecycle and Kubernetes reconciliation. The preceding increment qualifies the custom-control topology parcel with a route rule and resolved hierarchy site UUID through native lifecycle and Kubernetes reconciliation. The preceding increment qualifies service and transport Ethernet port-channel member-link parcels using their conditional payload branches. The preceding increment qualifies service and transport BGP parcels with AS number, router ID, and one IPv4 or IPv6 neighbor and advertised network, plus their VPN associations. Redistribution and policy references remain outside these fixtures. The preceding increment qualifies a non-tunnel WAN cellular parcel and its IPv4 tracker and tracker-group associations. The pinned provider points the group association to tracker/, but Manager actually stores and reads it at trackergroup/; CVK uses the observed Manager path. The preceding increment qualifies the non-tunnel WAN Ethernet parcel and all four IPv4/IPv6 tracker and tracker-group associations through native lifecycle and live Kubernetes reconciliation. Manager requires IPv6 settings on the parent before an IPv6 tracker can be associated. The preceding increment qualifies service and transport IPsec interface parcels and a transport IPsec-to-IPv4-tracker association. Both use a variable preshared-key reference and passed native lifecycle plus live Kubernetes reconciliation. The preceding increment qualifies service and transport GRE interface parcels and a transport GRE-to-IPv4-tracker association through native lifecycle and live Kubernetes reconciliation. The preceding increment qualifies Ethernet interface associations to IPv4 trackers and tracker groups through native lifecycle and live Kubernetes reconciliation. The preceding increment qualifies a service LAN VPN Ethernet interface and its three-level DHCP-server association through native lifecycle and live Kubernetes reconciliation. The Ethernet fixture covers IPv4 addressing and ARP; NAT, port-channel, VRRP, ACL, TrustSec and other advanced branches remain outside that fixture. The preceding increment qualifies the three-level service LAN VPN SVI-to-DHCP association. The preceding increment qualified a service LAN VPN SVI child with IPv4/IPv6 addressing, ARP and MTU. VRRP, ACL references and DHCP attachment remain pending. The preceding increment qualified six service and transport VPN routing associations: OSPF, EIGRP, multicast, and service OSPFv3 IPv4/IPv6. Each resolved its parent VPN and referenced routing parcel IDs through the Manager before association. The preceding increment qualified the core service LAN VPN parent and dual-router HA with a resolved VPN reference. The LAN VPN compiler currently accepts ID, name, OMP distance, DNS, host mapping, and IPv4/IPv6 next-hop and null-route fields; NAT, advertisements, route leaking and child interfaces are still outstanding. The preceding increment qualified the transport management VPN Ethernet child and its nested Manager path. The preceding increment qualified the transport management and WAN VPN parent parcels with native lifecycle and live Kubernetes reconciliation. The fixtures cover DNS, host mappings, IPv4 and IPv6 static routes, WAN ECMP, NAT64 pools, and the TE service. Interface children and device activation remain pending. The preceding increments qualified route policies, IPv4 and IPv6 ACLs, topology mesh and hub-and-spoke, and system device access. Policy-object references compile and order locally but need a lab where CVK can create the singleton policy-object profile; this lab already has one.

The previous increment qualified seven declarations: classic SVI, cellular and switchport templates, service EIGRP, service switchport, service multicast, and Zscaler SSE. Each passed native live create/read/update/read with cleanup and Kubernetes reconciliation. Qualification covers unattached fixture attributes, not router behavior or full parity. The previous increment qualified six routing/security declarations and six earlier tracker/SSE/SIG definitions.

docs.text:
For each row, run native create/read/update/read/idempotence and receipt-bound cleanup, followed by Kubernetes reconciliation with the selected fixture. Include dependency creation order, missing-reference behavior and resolved IDs for reference-bearing parcels. Do not attach these fixtures to routers as part of object qualification.

All 32 policy-object child declarations passed native create/read/update/delete under the existing Manager policy-object profile using isolated CVK names. The original parent child-ID set was verified after cleanup for each fixture. The singleton profile itself remains unqualified: CVK does not adopt or update the existing lab profile, so its creation still needs an empty test Manager.

docs.title: Native test commands
docs.text:
Provide Manager credentials through the existing environment/secret mechanism. The transport example below has passed; use the table above to select remaining fixtures. Select one fixture at a time, starting with absent fixture names.

CVK_SDWAN_LIVE=1 CVK_SDWAN_MUTATE=1 \
CVK_SDWAN_PENDING_FIXTURE=transport-trackers \
go test ./internal/controlleradapter/sdwan -run "^TestLivePendingLifecycle$" -count=1 -v

# On a Manager with one existing policy-object profile, child fixtures can
# be tested without creating or updating that parent. Run one fixture at a time.
CVK_SDWAN_LIVE=1 CVK_SDWAN_MUTATE=1 \
CVK_SDWAN_POLICY_FIXTURE=policy-security \
go test ./internal/controlleradapter/sdwan -run "^TestLiveExistingPolicyObjectChildren$" -count=1 -v

# On a lab whose vSmart meets the prerequisites above, select one activation
# fixture at a time. The test verifies an empty baseline and registers cleanup
# before sending the deployment request.
CVK_SDWAN_LIVE=1 CVK_SDWAN_MUTATE=1 \
CVK_SDWAN_ACTIVATION_FIXTURE=topology-group-activation \
go test ./internal/controlleradapter/sdwan -run "^TestLiveActivationLifecycle$" -count=1 -v

# KUBEBUILDER_ASSETS points to the Kubernetes 1.35.0 envtest binaries.
CVK_SDWAN_LIVE=1 CVK_SDWAN_ENVTEST_LIVE=1 \
CVK_SDWAN_ENVTEST_FIXTURE=transport-trackers.yaml \
go test -tags envtest ./internal/controlleradapter/sdwan -run TestEnvtest -count=1 -v

For the existing policy-profile.yaml fixture use TestLivePolicyProfileLifecycle. All examples have report-mode companion NetworkControllerConfig manifests.

docs.text: sdwan_other_trustsec_feature: Manager 20.18 requires sxpNodeId, absent from the pinned provider model; its empty device-password default is also rejected. The compiler rejects this fixture before mutation. Fixing the compatibility mapping and passing live tests are both still required.

docs.title: Broader deployment validation
docs.text: Device attachment, policy/topology activation, operational routing/forwarding, asynchronous recovery, pruning and import remain implementation and qualification work. The optional TestLiveActivationLifecycle has baseline checks and a restoration cleanup registered before activation; its current lab attempts failed at the prerequisites recorded above. Object CRUD tests do not qualify these workflows.

docs.title: SD-WAN controller deployment
docs.text:
Alpha · introduced in v2026.11.1. Use matching CRDs, chart and image; October v2026.10.0 does not contain this adapter. Check the release records for publication and artifact availability.

The independent sdwan adapter uses the existing CVK NetworkController worker and NetworkControllerConfig intent APIs. It calls SD-WAN Manager directly; the NetAsCode module and provider are source references for porting the data model, schemas, defaults and API behavior. Terraform is not a build, test or deployment dependency of the SD-WAN integration.

This implementation is a fixture-qualified increment, not full NetAsCode parity. The pinned upstream module has 226 resource declarations. 181 resource declarations have fixture-level native live coverage on Manager 20.18.2.2:

The provider is CiscoDevNet/sdwan; netascode/terraform-sdwan-nac-sdwan is the module. internal/controlleradapter/sdwan/testdata/upstream-lock.json records every resource declaration and distinguishes fixture-qualified coverage from pending coverage. Qualification applies to the fixture's attributes, not every attribute of that resource type.

An additional 7 declarations have native implementations but remain unqualified: the policy-object singleton profile, system CA certificates, custom applications (the lab lacks SD-AVC), cloud-provider settings (the lab already has the singleton), device-template attachment, centralized policy activation and topology-group activation. SIG credential creation now passes after fixing the global flag and variable-secret payloads. Site/router tag association passed live on BR-2-WAN with removal and cleanup. Configuration and policy group association also passed live on that router, but device deployment has not been pushed. All 32 policy-object child declarations passed native lifecycle on Manager 20.18 under its existing singleton profile, with the original child-ID set restored after each fixture. The profile itself remains unqualified because the lab already has one. No resource declarations remain pending; TrustSec remains compatibility-blocked. This inventory does not imply full field-level parity or router deployment qualification. See the implementation and live-test backlog for the complete list, fixture paths and prerequisites.

docs.title: Model contract
docs.text:
The public model remains the upstream sdwan document. The format is netascode-sdwan, model version 1.5.0. The compiler currently supports:

  • edge_feature_templates.banner_templates: name, description, device types, login/MOTD literals and variables, including upstream device-type defaults.
  • edge_feature_templates.cli_templates, global_settings_templates, multicast_templates, cellular_controller_templates and cellular_profile_templates, bfd_templates, igmp_templates, ntp_templates, omp_templates, pim_templates, thousandeyes_templates, secure_app_hosting_templates, dhcp_server_templates, ipsec_interface_templates, snmp_templates, logging_templates and gre_interface_templates, including per-family device defaults and overrides. Generate their metadata with scripts/sdwan/generate-classic-definitions.py MODULE_CHECKOUT PROVIDER_CHECKOUT.
  • feature_profiles.system_profiles: profile name/description, banner, basic, BFD, global, OMP, NTP, logging, MRF, flexible port speed, performance monitoring, security, SNMP and AAA. feature_profiles.cli_profiles.config supports native CLI parcels. Scalar and nested-list definitions for basic/global/OMP/NTP/logging/security are generated from pinned module mappings and provider defaults/value schemas. Regenerate with scripts/sdwan/generate-parcel-definitions.py MODULE_CHECKOUT PROVIDER_CHECKOUT. Generated metadata retains the upstream MPL-2.0 license in definitions/LICENSE.
  • feature_profiles.transport_profiles.gps_features and other_profiles.ucse / other_profiles.thousandeyes, including the NaC GPS enable default and the ThousandEyes virtual-application wrapper. These fixtures are unattached.
  • feature_profiles.service_profiles.dhcp_servers, ipv4_trackers and object_trackers, ipv4_tracker_groups and object_tracker_groups, with native name-based parcel management and full generated API-data schema checks for these resources.
  • feature_profiles.transport_profiles.cellular_controllers and cellular_profiles, including authentication switches, credential variables and network slicing on the qualified 20.18 Manager. Inactive authentication fields and invalid slicing combinations are rejected before mutation.
  • configuration_groups: name/description and references to declared system, transport, service, CLI or other profiles. Device associations are not enabled.
  • Name/description mappings for the other eight profile collections, plus the automatically created application-priority settings parcel and visibility flags.
  • All 24 classic policy_objects collections, including named SLA probe references. Policy names are limited to 32 characters because this Manager rewrites longer names.
  • application_catalog.custom_applications: custom names, server names, L3/L4 rows and business relevance; the lab cannot qualify create until SD-AVC is enabled.
  • network_hierarchy groups/regions through levels 0–2 and unassigned sites with the 20.18 location/GPS model. Global collectors remain unsupported.

deployment.yaml combines the baseline fixtures under one config and five managed sections. Use deployment-config.yaml with its resolved output instead of installing individual configs that would compete for the same section Lease. The combined fixture includes hierarchy prerequisites for region lists. For policy-objects-config.yaml, resolve policy-deployment.yaml so that the region prerequisite is included. system-features-config.yaml uses system-features.yaml as an alternative feature-profile section owner. The compiler allows up to 512 resources, bounded to 128 per section by journal capacity.

Unknown fields and unsupported sections fail before mutation. Credentials and intent Secret injection are separate concerns: endpoint credentials work through projected files; intent secretRefs are currently rejected rather than ignored. No controller-specific API payloads appear in the public CRD.

Resolve the qualified defaults outside the worker before declaring the source resolved. This retains upstream field names:

go run ./cmd/cvk-sdwan-resolve examples/configs/sdwan/banner.yaml > /tmp/sdwan-banner.json
go run ./cmd/cvk-sdwan-resolve examples/configs/sdwan/system-profile.yaml > /tmp/sdwan-system-profile.json

docs.title: Deploy the qualified fixtures
docs.text:
Install a matching CVK image and Helm chart. The chart adds the dedicated cisco-virtual-kubelet-sdwan-worker ClusterRole. Its namespace-scoped binding grants status updates and section Lease get/create/update; it grants no Secret API access, device mutation permission, or remote-deletion permission.

Create the sdwan-lab namespace and a same-namespace sdwan-credentials Secret with username and password keys using your existing secret-management process. Do not put credentials into the model or commit them to the repository.

kubectl create namespace sdwan-lab
kubectl apply -f examples/configs/sdwan/controller.yaml
kubectl -n sdwan-lab create configmap sdwan-banner-fixture \
  --from-file=model.yaml=/tmp/sdwan-banner.json
kubectl -n sdwan-lab create configmap sdwan-system-profile-fixture \
  --from-file=model.yaml=/tmp/sdwan-system-profile.json
kubectl apply -f examples/configs/sdwan/banner-config.yaml
kubectl apply -f examples/configs/sdwan/system-profile-config.yaml
kubectl -n sdwan-lab get networkcontrollers,networkcontrollerconfigs

The examples initially report drift. Select spec.mode: apply to deploy the fixtures. Expect incremental Applying status followed by InSync after read-back verification. Reconciliation preserves existing matching resources without resubmitting their creation. An external object with the same name is a collision, not implicit authorization to adopt it.

The lab manifest explicitly opts into insecure TLS because this endpoint's self-signed certificate has no IP SAN. Other deployments should supply a valid certificate and trust bundle. Sessions remain in process memory, rotate with projected material, and have bounded lifetimes. Redirects are rejected; only GET may refresh and retry after 401. Error bodies, cookies and tokens are not logged.

docs.title: Ownership and recovery
docs.text:
Ownership is per controller UID, global scope and managed section. One config incarnation owns each section; separate configs cannot split the same section. Each worker session holds a 90-second Lease. Before a remote mutation, the worker persists a Dispatched receipt and rechecks the live endpoint/config/source and Lease bindings. A successful response persists the remote ID before verification.

A settled Lease can transfer to a replacement worker for the same config after expiry. An unresolved dispatch blocks takeover and automatic replay. Such a failure requires investigation; an automatic uncertain-outcome recovery workflow is not implemented. Status reports OutcomeUnknown or SectionOwned without raw controller payloads. Never clear the journal merely to retry a timed-out POST.

Retain is the supported prune/deletion policy. Deleting intent retains remote objects and its ownership journal; deletion does not transfer ownership to a new config UID. Remote pruning, explicit adoption/import, ownership release and live qualification of device attachment/activation is still pending; activation attempts reached Manager but failed on lab prerequisites. The fixture test harness cleans up only its own created IDs in reverse dependency order.

docs.title: Native CVK tests
docs.text:
Normal tests do not contact the lab. Live tests require explicit environment flags and credentials supplied outside Git. The test harness creates temporary credential projections and removes them at completion.

go test ./internal/controlleradapter/...
go test -race ./internal/controlleradapter/... ./cmd/cisco-vk
# KUBEBUILDER_ASSETS must point to Kubernetes 1.35.0 test binaries.
go test -tags envtest ./internal/controlleradapter/sdwan -run TestEnvtest -v

Live native lifecycle tests use CVK_SDWAN_LIVE=1 and CVK_SDWAN_MUTATE=1, with SDWAN_URL, SDWAN_USERNAME, SDWAN_PASSWORD and the appropriate TLS setting supplied outside Git. Select the intended TestLive*Lifecycle test explicitly. Live Kubernetes tests additionally use CVK_SDWAN_ENVTEST_LIVE=1 and select a fixture through CVK_SDWAN_ENVTEST_FIXTURE. These tests exercise CVK's native compiler, API client and reconciliation.

docs.title: Remaining deployment parity
docs.text:
Although all pinned resource declarations have CVK implementations, full upstream field/default coverage, advanced classic device-template children, routing and transport/service branches, live qualification of modern policy-object parcels, device attachment/deployment, asynchronous activation recovery, pruning and import are not complete. Reproducible device-level qualification also needs explicit WAN-edge targets and a restoration policy. The BR-2-WAN tag and group association tests used the selected lab router and restored its prior state.

See the qualification record for measured results and limits.

docs.title: Manager 20.18 TrustSec incompatibility
docs.text: The pinned provider's TrustSec payload is rejected because data.sxpNodeId is required by this Manager but absent from the provider model. Its default empty devicePassword is also rejected. The reproducible fixture is under examples/configs/sdwan/unqualified/trustsec.yaml; the compiler rejects TrustSec before mutation. Generated TrustSec metadata is retained for further compatibility work and does not count toward qualified coverage.

docs.title: Policy-object profile qualification
docs.text:
policy-profile.yaml defines the singular policy-object profile and fifteen policy parcels. policy-prefixes.yaml, policy-dependencies.yaml and policy-security.yaml exercise the remaining modern policy-object declarations. All 32 child declarations passed native lifecycle under the lab's existing singleton profile; every fixture restored the original child-ID set. CVK did not update or adopt the parent. Creating the singleton profile itself remains unqualified because the lab already has one; that test needs an empty Manager.

The pinned module uses forwarding_classes where the current documentation calls this collection class_maps. This branch follows the pinned module's name. NaC integer queue and TLOC preference values are encoded as strings for the provider API, with their public numeric constraints retained.

The pinned module's SNMP groups[].view_variable expression incorrectly traverses group.view.view_variable. That unavailable input is explicitly rejected. AAA accounting_rules[].start_stop_variable is passed verbatim by the module and therefore requires the upstream {{variable}} expression. Other generated parcel variable fields wrap the public variable name as required by their module mapping.

docs.title: Classic PIM provider limitation
docs.text: The pinned provider does not serialize pim_templates[].rp_addresses[].optional. CVK rejects this field before mutation; the qualified fixture omits it. Other PIM row types preserve their optional flag and provider-defined priority order.

docs.title: Tracker references and classic logging compatibility
docs.text:
Tracker groups require two distinct tracker names declared in the same service profile. CVK creates trackers before groups, resolves controller IDs before every write and comparison, and rejects missing dependencies without sending a mutation.

The pinned module reads version_ciphersuites_variablevariable for classic logging TLS ciphersuite variables. CVK rejects that typo and ciphersuites_variable; literal ciphersuites is fixture-qualified. Classic IPsec supports nested ike/ipsec fields and the numeric DH-group form shown in the NaC example.
